arXiv:2610.06415v1 [cs.LG] 05 Oct 2026

Training-Free Transformer Merging via Sequential
Local Operator Alignment

Akansh Maurya Affiliation: CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security    Ya-Wei Eileen Lin Affiliation: Munich Center for Machine Learning Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, School of Computation, Information and Technology    Stefanie Jegelka Affiliation: Munich Center for Machine Learning Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, School of Computation, Information and Technology Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Department of EECS, CSAIL   
Sebastian U. Stich Affiliation: CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security    Rotem Mulayoff Affiliation: CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security
Abstract

Training-free model merging aims to combine multiple fine-tuned models into a single model without further optimization on labeled data. Yet, in transformers, independently merging individual layers can affect a shared attention computation because the query–key and value–output operators depend on composed matrices, overlooking the functional structure. Moreover, when merging earlier components, downstream components receive different activations than they do in the original model, thus, the merged and original execution paths no longer match. In this paper, we introduce Sequential Local Operator Alignment, a training-free method that merges transformers along the execution path of the partially merged model. Our method uses calibration data to estimate the local behavior of each functional component, aligns operators sequentially under the intermediate activation of the partially merged model, and subsequently factorizes the merged operators back into valid transformer parameters. We empirically show that this sequential step reduces error accumulation across layers. Furthermore, the proposed operator factorization step enables rank expansion, providing a principled mechanism for increasing multi-task capacity. We demonstrate that our approach generalizes across modalities, model scales, and varying numbers of tasks, from CLIP and RoBERTa to billion-parameter LLMs, and further extends naturally to the merging of LoRA-fine-tuned models. The results indicate improvements over strong merging baselines without requiring rank expansion, while optional expansion provides a further accuracy–inference-cost trade-off. Project link: https://akansh12.github.io/SLOA-Merge/

1 Introduction

Modern neural networks are often adapted into many task-specific variants from the same pretrained initialization (Bommasani et al., 2021; Devlin et al., 2019; Raffel et al., 2020; Radford et al., 2021a; Ding et al., 2023). However, maintaining a separate model for every task is expensive (Guo et al., 2021; Wortsman et al., 2022; Yadav et al., 2025), while retraining a single multi-task model can require substantial data, compute, and engineering effort (Ruder, 2017; Crawshaw, 2020; Yang et al., 2024b). Training-free model merging (Xu et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2025; Matena and Raffel, 2022; Ilharco et al., 2023; Ortiz-Jimenez et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2023) provides a practical alternative: given several independently fine-tuned models, the goal is to combine them into one model without further training. An effective merged model should preserve the task-specific capabilities of the original models while offering the deployment efficiency of a single network (Yang et al., 2026).

Many existing training-free merging methods operate directly on individual parameter tensors or individual activation spaces. For example, they average corresponding weight matrices (Wortsman et al., 2022), interpolate task vectors (Ilharco et al., 2023), or align intermediate activations layer by layer (Ainsworth et al., 2023; Singh and Jaggi, 2020). While simple and often effective, this layer-wise perspective is parameterization-dependent: a model’s function is not uniquely tied to the particular tensors used to represent it (Zhao et al., 2025; Bürgin et al., 2026; Bona-Pellissier et al., 2023; Elhage et al., 2021; Dar et al., 2023). For instance, in a transformer attention head (Vaswani et al., 2017), the matrices 𝐖Q\mathbf{W}_{Q}, 𝐖K\mathbf{W}_{K}, 𝐖V\mathbf{W}_{V}, and 𝐖O\mathbf{W}_{O} are not used as independent functional units. The query and key determine the pre-softmax attention scores through the combined bilinear operator 𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤{\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top}, while the value and output determine the post-attention contribution through the composed operator 𝑾V​𝑾O{\bm{W}}_{V}{\bm{W}}_{O}. Thus, the functionally meaningful objects are the composed operators 𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤{\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top} and 𝑾V​𝑾O{\bm{W}}_{V}{\bm{W}}_{O}. A merging procedure that independently combines 𝐖Q\mathbf{W}_{Q} and 𝐖K\mathbf{W}_{K}, or 𝐖V\mathbf{W}_{V} and 𝐖O\mathbf{W}_{O}, may therefore fail to preserve a shared attention computation even when that computation is functionally equivalent.

A natural way is to merge objects at the level at which they enter the model’s computation, rather than at the level of an arbitrary parameter decomposition. To this end, we introduce Sequential Local Operator Alignment (SLOA), a training-free framework for merging transformer models by aligning local functional operators (see Fig. 1 for the illustration). SLOA associates each model component with the local operator. For each component, SLOA constructs a merged operator from the task models. SLOA considers two alignment criteria: (i) behavior matching, on calibration inputs to the component, the merged operator should produce outputs close to those of the task-specific operators, and (ii) data-aware operator regularization, the merged operator is kept close to the task-specific operators under a metric induced by the calibration activations. This metric emphasizes directions that are active on the data. Importantly, our contribution is to instantiate them as a unified local-operator alignment framework for training-free transformer merging. The same objective applies across LayerNorm modules, linear maps, QK attention operators, and VO attention operators by changing only the behavior map and the induced metric.

A key feature of our framework is that alignment is performed sequentially. When earlier operators have already been merged, the hidden activations entering later components are no longer identical to the activations produced by any individual task model. If later components are merged only under the original task-model activations, the local objective assumes that all previous merges were perfect. Our approach instead evaluates the activation-matching term on the activations produced by the partially merged model. This makes each local merge corrective, aligning downstream operators along the actual execution path of the merged network and reducing error accumulation across layers.

Our operator view separates the merged operator from its eventual factorization. For QK and VO components, each individual task head has rank at most the head dimension, but the merged multi-task operator may require a higher-rank representation, as different tasks can use different subspaces. Therefore, we treat rank as a capacity-control mechanism. After merging an operator, we can factorize it at the original rank to preserve the architecture, or expand the rank to retain additional singular directions that capture task-specific behavior. Empirically, our method achieves state-of-the-art training-free merging performance across vision benchmarks, RoBERTa models, and billion-parameter LLMs. Moreover, SLOA naturally extends to models fine-tuned with LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), further broadening its applicability to parameter-efficient adaptation settings. It consistently outperforms baselines that merge individual weights or rely on isolated activation alignment, supporting the central claim that model merging should be performed at local functional operators.

2 Motivation: limitations of isolated attention-weight merging

In a transformer attention head, the query, key, value, and output layers 𝑾Q{\bm{W}}_{Q}, 𝑾K{\bm{W}}_{K}, 𝑾V{\bm{W}}_{V}, and 𝑾O{\bm{W}}_{O} are often merged independently, or their corresponding intermediate activations are aligned separately. Given token activations 𝑿{\bm{X}}, the query and key weights determine the pre-softmax attention scores only through the composed QK operator 𝑴QK=𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤{\bm{M}}_{\mathrm{QK}}={\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top} and scores⁡(𝑿)=𝑿​𝑴QK​𝑿⊤\mathrm{scores}({\bm{X}})={\bm{X}}{\bm{M}}_{\mathrm{QK}}{\bm{X}}^{\top}. Similarly, for a fixed attention pattern 𝑨{\bm{A}}, the value and output weights determine the head contribution only through the composed VO operator 𝑴VO=𝑾V​𝑾O{\bm{M}}_{\mathrm{VO}}={\bm{W}}_{V}{\bm{W}}_{O} and head⁡(𝑿)=𝑨​𝑿​𝑴VO\mathrm{head}({\bm{X}})={\bm{A}}{\bm{X}}{\bm{M}}_{\mathrm{VO}}. Thus, the functional objects are the composed operators 𝑴QK{\bm{M}}_{\mathrm{QK}} and 𝑴VO{\bm{M}}_{\mathrm{VO}}, whereas the individual matrices 𝑾Q,𝑾K,𝑾V,𝑾O{\bm{W}}_{Q},{\bm{W}}_{K},{\bm{W}}_{V},{\bm{W}}_{O} are only one possible factorization of these operators.

Example 1. Consider two QK factorizations that represent the same attention-score operator 𝑴QK(1)=𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤{\bm{M}}_{\mathrm{QK}}^{(1)}={\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top}, and 𝑴QK(2)=(𝑾Q​𝑹)​(𝑾K​𝑹−⁣⊤)⊤=𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤{\bm{M}}_{\mathrm{QK}}^{(2)}=({\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{R}})({\bm{W}}_{K}{\bm{R}}^{-\top})^{\top}={\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top}. The multiplicative factor equals 11 only when c=1c=1, and it grows without bound as c→∞c\rightarrow\infty. Thus, for any input 𝑿{\bm{X}} s.t. The same argument applies to VO under (𝑾V​𝑹,𝑹−1​𝑾O)({\bm{W}}_{V}{\bm{R}},\ {\bm{R}}^{-1}{\bm{W}}_{O}). Our solution is to treat 𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤{\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top} (and 𝑾V​𝑾O{\bm{W}}_{V}{\bm{W}}_{O}) as a single unit for merging (Fig. 2) and re-factorize after merging. This has two advantages: (1) we forgo the parameterization ambiguity and any search for a good aligning transformation; (2) the rank of the merged operator can be chosen freely at factorization time, allowing us to adjust capacity.

3 Methodology: Sequential local operator alignment (SLOA)

The above example shows that independent merging can produce arbitrary functional errors when computation is performed inside a transformer. To address this, we introduce Sequential Local Operator Alignment, a training-free method that merges models by aligning the local functional operators.

3.1 Local functional operators

We define local functional operators as the parameterized object that determines a component’s local computation once its input activation and any non-learned part are fixed. For example, the local operator of a linear layer is its weight matrix, while the local operator of an attention head is more naturally expressed through the composed QK and VO operators (see Fig. 1).

We write 𝜽\bm{\theta} for a generic local operator and 𝒜⁡(𝒁,𝜽)\mathcal{A}({\bm{Z}};\bm{\theta}) for its behavior map, where 𝒁{\bm{Z}} denotes the local input needed to evaluate the operator. For most operators, 𝒁{\bm{Z}} is the activation 𝑿{\bm{X}}, and for VO, it includes both the attention matrix and the residual state. Table 1 summarizes the local functional operators used in our transformer merging procedure. The key design criterion is that, for fixed local input 𝒁{\bm{Z}}, the behavior map 𝒜⁡(𝒁,𝜽)\mathcal{A}({\bm{Z}};\bm{\theta}) is linear in the local operator 𝜽\bm{\theta}. Specifically, LayerNorm is linear in (𝜸,𝜷)(\bm{\gamma},\bm{\beta}) after the normalization statistics are fixed; a linear layer is linear in 𝑾{\bm{W}}; QK is linear in the composed score operator 𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤/dk.{\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{k}}.; and VO is linear in the composed operator 𝑾V​𝑾O{\bm{W}}_{V}{\bm{W}}_{O}.

The same template can be applied beyond the operators in Table 1 whenever a module admits a local representation that is linear in the chosen operator. For example, in a gated MLP, the down-projection can be treated as a local linear operator after the gated hidden activation has been formed. Operators that remain nonlinear in their parameters after conditioning on the local input would require either a smaller linear suboperator or an additional approximation, which are not the focus of this work.

3.2 Activation-based local behavior matching

Suppose we merge TT task-specific models. For a fixed local operator, let 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t} denote the corresponding operator in model tt, and let ntn_{t} be the number of calibration samples for that model. For calibration example ii, let 𝒁t,i{\bm{Z}}_{t,i} be the local input received by the operator when running the original task model tt, and let 𝒁^t,i\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i} be the local input received by the same operator when running the partially merged model. We also define the corresponding local state collections χt={𝒁t,i}i=1nt\chi_{t}=\{{\bm{Z}}_{t,i}\}_{i=1}^{n_{t}} and χ^t={𝒁^t,i}i=1nt\widehat{\chi}_{t}=\{\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\}_{i=1}^{n_{t}}.

The task-model output for this local operator is 𝒜⁡(𝒁t,i,𝜽t)\mathcal{A}({\bm{Z}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta}_{t}), while the merged operator, evaluated on the state it will actually receive during the merged model’s forward pass, produces 𝒜⁡(𝒁^t,i,𝜽)\mathcal{A}(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta}). Thus, the activation-based local alignment loss is then given by

(2) ℒact​(𝜽)=1T​∑t=1T1nt​∑i=1nt‖𝒜⁡(𝒁^t,i,𝜽)−𝒜⁡(𝒁t,i,𝜽t)‖F2.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\left\|\mathcal{A}(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta})-\mathcal{A}({\bm{Z}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta}_{t})\right\|_{F}^{2}.

Equivalently, Eq. (2) first samples a model uniformly from {1,…,T}\{1,\ldots,T\} and then samples a calibration example uniformly from that model. This balanced empirical average prevents models with more calibration examples from dominating the local objective. Note that Eq. (2) is functional: the merged operator is asked to reproduce the local outputs of the task-specific operators. However, with a small calibration set, activation matching alone can be underdetermined. Many operators may agree on the observed local activations while behaving differently on unobserved activations. We therefore add a data-dependent weight-space geometry term introduced in the next subsection.

3.3 Data-dependent weight geometry

Pure weight-space merging is stable and sample-efficient, but it treats all parameter directions as equally important. Pure activation matching focuses on functionality, but with only a small calibration set, it can be underdetermined and sensitive to the observed samples. SLOA considers these two views jointly: the activation term matches local behavior, while the geometry term keeps the merged operator close to the task-specific operators in directions that are important under the calibrations. For a standard one-sided linear operator, such as 𝑿​𝑾{\bm{X}}{\bm{W}}, we define

Here, ϕ⁡(χ^t)\phi(\widehat{\chi}_{t}) denotes the collection of token-level vectors that multiply the operator in the local behavior map. Here, Θamb\Theta_{\mathrm{amb}} is the ambient operator space. For linear maps and LayerNorm affine parameters, this is the usual parameter space. For QK and VO operators, Θamb=ℝd×d\Theta_{\mathrm{amb}}=\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is the residual-space operator space; the rank constraint induced by attention-head width is imposed later during factorization. Because 𝒜⁡(𝒁^,𝜽)\mathcal{A}(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}};\bm{\theta}) is linear in 𝜽\bm{\theta} for fixed calibration states, Eq. (5) is a quadratic objective. Thus, each local operator can be merged by solving a closed-form regularized least-squares problem. Further derivations of the local operator alignment optimal solutions are in §D.

3.4 Sequential merging

The objective in Eq. (5) is applied sequentially. Let 𝒪\mathcal{O} be the set of local operators and write oa≺obo_{a}\prec o_{b} if the output or activation produced by operator oao_{a} can affect the input to operator obo_{b}. We choose a topological order o1,o2,…,oMo_{1},o_{2},\ldots,o_{M} that is in line with this dependency relation. At step mm, the operators o1,…,om−1o_{1},\ldots,o_{m-1} have been merged. For each model tt and calibration ii, we have two local inputs for omo_{m}. First, 𝒁t,i(m){\bm{Z}}_{t,i}^{(m)} is the local input produced by the original task model tt. Second, 𝒁^t,i(m)\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{(m)} is the local input produced by the partially merged model, whose predecessors o1,…,om−1o_{1},\ldots,o_{m-1} use the merged operators. The current operator is then merged by solving Eq. (5) with 𝒁t,i=𝒁t,i(m){\bm{Z}}_{t,i}={\bm{Z}}_{t,i}^{(m)}, 𝒁^t,i=𝒁^t,i(m)\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}=\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{(m)}, and 𝜽t=𝜽t(m)\bm{\theta}_{t}=\bm{\theta}_{t}^{(m)}. This sequential construction is important. If the current operator were aligned only on 𝒁t,i(m){\bm{Z}}_{t,i}^{(m)}, the local objective would implicitly assume that all previous operators had been merged perfectly. In practice, earlier merging steps may shift the activations seen by later operators. By evaluating 𝒁^t,i(m)\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{(m)}, SLOA aligns each operator on the activation distribution that it will actually receive inside the partially merged model. The target remains 𝒜⁡(𝒁t,i(m),𝜽t(m))\mathcal{A}({\bm{Z}}_{t,i}^{(m)};\bm{\theta}_{t}^{(m)}), therefore, the current operator corrects for accumulated upstream error while preserving the task-specific local behavior.

3.5 Rank as capacity control

Our method allows the merged model to have a larger capacity than the task-specific models. For example, let 𝑾Q,𝑾K,𝑾V∈ℝd×dk{\bm{W}}_{Q},{\bm{W}}_{K},{\bm{W}}_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{k}} and 𝑾O∈ℝdk×d{\bm{W}}_{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times d} be the parameters for an attention head from the task-specific models, then the local operators for this head are given by

(6) 𝜽Q​K=𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤/dkand𝜽V​O=𝑾V​𝑾O,s.t.𝜽Q​K,𝜽V​O∈ℝd×d.\bm{\theta}_{QK}={\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{k}}\quad\text{and}\quad\bm{\theta}_{VO}={\bm{W}}_{V}{\bm{W}}_{O},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\bm{\theta}_{QK},\bm{\theta}_{VO}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}.

Since these operators are realized through a width-dkd_{k} bottleneck, they have rank at most dkd_{k}. The merged operator, however, needs to combine TT such operators that may occupy different subspaces. Consequently, it is likely that using the same model width for the merged model, i.e., a rank of at most dkd_{k}, would result in underfitting. Therefore, it is important to let the merged model be more expressive, which in this case means a rank exceeding dkd_{k}. To this end, note that SLOA solves for 𝜽merge∈ℝd×d\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} without any constraints, while the factorization rank rr for the merged parameters is chosen only afterward. Let 𝜽merger=𝑼r​𝚺r​𝑽r⊤\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}^{r}={\bm{U}}_{r}{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r}{\bm{V}}_{r}^{\top} be the best rank-rr approximation of 𝜽merge\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}, and

(7) QK:𝑾¯Q=𝑼r​(τ​𝚺r)1/2,𝑾¯K=𝑽r​(τ​𝚺r)1/2,VO:𝑾¯V=𝑼r​𝚺r1/2,𝑾¯O=𝚺r1/2​𝑽r⊤,s.t.𝑾¯Q,𝑾¯K∈ℝd×r,𝑾¯V∈ℝd×r,𝑾¯O∈ℝr×d,\begin{aligned} \text{QK:}&\quad\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{Q}={\bm{U}}_{r}(\tau{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r})^{1/2},&&\ \bar{{\bm{W}}}_{K}={\bm{V}}_{r}(\tau{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r})^{1/2},\\ \text{VO:}&\quad\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{V}={\bm{U}}_{r}{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r}^{1/2},&&\ \bar{{\bm{W}}}_{O}={\bm{\Sigma}}_{r}^{1/2}{\bm{V}}_{r}^{\top},\end{aligned}\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad\begin{aligned} &\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{Q},\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r},\\ &\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r},\ \bar{{\bm{W}}}_{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d},\end{aligned}

where τ=r\tau=\sqrt{r} is the attention scaling. With this choice of parameters for the merged model, we have 𝑾¯Q​𝑾¯K⊤/τ=𝜽merge,Q​Kr\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{Q}\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{K}^{\top}/\tau=\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge},QK}^{r} and 𝑾¯V​𝑾¯O=𝜽merge,V​Or\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{V}\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{O}=\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge},VO}^{r}, where the rank of the merged head operators is rr. Setting r=dkr=d_{k} preserves the architecture, whereas r>dkr>d_{k} increases the rank of each head. Naturally, adding more parameters to the model increases the computational cost at inference. Empirically, we find that moderately increasing the rank improves performance while incurring only a small computational overhead. Further discussion about rank expansion in §D.5.

Additional remarks. We conclude this section with two remarks: (i) RegMean (Jin et al., 2023) regularizes each linear-layer weight through Gram-matrix shrinkage. However, in attention, similar projection matrices do not necessarily imply similar computations. For example, changes to the query and key matrices can cancel each other and leave the QK operator unchanged, even though a penalty on the two matrices would still be nonzero. We build 𝚲t{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t} from calibration states of the partially merged model. The resulting metric, 𝚲t⊗𝚲t{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\otimes{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}, weights differences in the QK operator along both inputs to the attention-score map. Unlike separate penalties on 𝑾Q{\bm{W}}_{Q} and 𝑾K{\bm{W}}_{K}, it constrains the computation they define together while keeping the objective quadratic in the operator variable. Thus, SLOA keeps the local operators close to their task-specific counterparts without forcing their internal attention factors to use the same coordinates. (ii) ProDistill (Xu et al., 2025) progressively matches block outputs on paired partially merged and task-model activations by optimizing element-wise task-vector coefficients. SLOA shares this progressive matching principle, but changes both the merging variables and the level at which behavior is matched. Specifically, it aligns composed QK and VO operators through pre-softmax score matching and attention-weighted output matching, respectively. For fixed local inputs, these behavior maps are linear, yielding quadratic alignment objectives that can be solved with structured linear algebra. Merely replacing projection factors with composed operators in a block-level distillation objective would not yield this property.

Importantly, the main novelty of SLOA over existing methods is that SLOA treats merging as a sequence of operator-level regression problems. At each step, it matches local behavior, regularizes the operators using the data, and reconstructs them at a chosen rank. As it works directly with the composed QK and VO operators, it does not depend on how these operators are factorized. It also lets us choose the rank used by the deployed model, giving the merged model greater capacity.

4 Experiments

In this section, we demonstrate SLOA for model merging across vision, natural language understanding, and large language model settings, using both fully fine-tuned and LoRA-adapted experts. In §4.1, we evaluate Vision Transformers (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) on image classification benchmarks comprising 8, 14, and 20 tasks, focusing on the ViT-B/32 architecture. In §4.2, we consider merging RoBERTa models (Liu et al., 2019) for natural language understanding (NLU). Finally, in §4.3, we evaluate SLOA at a larger model scale by merging LoRA-adapted LLaMA-2-7B experts (Touvron et al., 2023) trained for math, code, and instruction-following tasks. Fig. 3 previews the per-task gains of SLOA over all baselines. Unless otherwise stated, all training-free methods that require calibration, including SLOA, use N=256N{=}256 samples per task drawn exclusively from the corresponding training split; no test data is used for merging. All results are averaged over three random seeds. Additional experiments in §F, and full experimental details are provided in §E.

4.1 Merging Vision Transformers (ViT-B)

We first evaluate SLOA on multi-task merging of ViT-B/32 experts using the task-specific checkpoints provided by Tang et al. (2024). All experts are fine-tuned from a shared CLIP initialization (Radford et al., 2021b), each on a distinct image classification task. We consider three increasingly challenging settings involving 8, 14, and 20 experts. Our data-free baselines are weight averaging (Wortsman et al., 2022), Task Arithmetic (Ilharco et al., 2023), TIES-Merging (Yadav et al., 2023), TSV-M (Gargiulo et al., 2025), and Iso-C and Iso-CTS (Marczak et al., 2025). We also compare against training-free methods that use calibration data: Fisher Merging (Matena and Raffel, 2022), RegMean (Jin et al., 2023), and RegMean++ (Nguyen et al., 2026).

Table 2 summarizes the results. At the original rank, SLOA outperforms all baselines across the three settings. Its advantage over the strongest baseline, RegMean++, increases with the number of merged tasks, from 0.60.6 percentage points for 8 tasks to 1.91.9 for 14 tasks and 5.55.5 for 20 tasks. These results demonstrate that SLOA handles an increasing number of tasks more effectively than the competing methods on these benchmarks.

Our component ablations suggest that sequential alignment accounts for most of the improvement by compensating for upstream merging errors that subsequent operators would otherwise inherit (See §F.4 and §F.7). Merging the composed QK and VO operators yields a further, consistent gain over sequential alignment alone. The operator formulation also enables rank expansion. Increasing the retained rank from r=64r{=}64, the original head dimension, to r=128r{=}128 improves accuracy across all three settings, with larger gains when merging more tasks. This suggests that model capacity increasingly constrains merging performance as the number of tasks grows. We use a fixed calibration budget of N=256N{=}256 and report retained ranks of r=64r{=}64 and r=128r{=}128 to provide a controlled comparison and assess the benefit of rank expansion. These choices do not represent limits of SLOA: larger calibration sets and retained ranks yield further improvements, at the cost of additional merging time and, for rank expansion, additional inference time (§F.3 and §G). We observe similar trends for ViT-B/16 (§F.1) and LoRA fine-tuned models (§F.2).

4.2 Merging encoder-based language models

To assess whether operator alignment extends beyond vision, we merge seven RoBERTa-base models fine-tuned on distinct GLUE tasks (Wang et al., 2019), using the checkpoints provided by Yu et al. (2024). These tasks cover linguistic acceptability (CoLA), sentiment classification (SST-2), paraphrase and question-pair matching (MRPC, QQP), and textual entailment (MNLI, QNLI, RTE), requiring the merged model to preserve task-specific computations across diverse input structures and decision boundaries. We compare SLOA against the same baselines used in the ViT experiment.

As shown in Table 3, SLOA at the original rank (r=64r{=}64) improves the average score over the strongest baseline by 7.77.7 points. Increasing the QK/VO rank to r=128r{=}128 improves scores on every task and raises this margin to 8.48.4 points. The gains extend across the benchmark: SLOA achieves the highest scores on six of the seven tasks (CoLA, SST-2, MRPC, MNLI, QNLI, and RTE), trailing only TIES-Merging and TSV-M on QQP (per-task results in Table 16). These findings are consistent with the motivation for aligning composed attention operators. The coupled QK and VO operators govern token interactions and value transformations within each attention head; aligning them can help preserve the distinct attention patterns learned by experts fine-tuned on different language tasks.

4.3 Merging LLaMA-2-7B LoRA experts

SLOA applies directly to LoRA-adapted experts without modifying its local objective. For each task tt, we first form the effective fine-tuned weight 𝑾t=𝑾0+𝑩t​𝑨t\bm{W}_{t}=\bm{W}_{0}+\bm{B}_{t}\bm{A}_{t} and then construct the same functional operators used for fully fine-tuned experts. This approach also avoids the factorization ambiguity of LoRA: since 𝑩t​𝑨t=(𝑩t​𝑹)​(𝑹−1​𝑨t)\bm{B}_{t}\bm{A}_{t}=(\bm{B}_{t}\bm{R})(\bm{R}^{-1}\bm{A}_{t}) for any invertible 𝑹\bm{R}, merging 𝑨t\bm{A}_{t} and 𝑩t\bm{B}_{t} separately can make the result depend on an arbitrary choice of low-rank coordinates. By operating on the effective weights and their composed operators, SLOA is invariant to this ambiguity.

We evaluate this setting by merging three LoRA-adapted LLaMA-2-7B experts specialized in math, code, and instruction-following (details in §E.2.3). LLaMA-2 is a decoder-only architecture with rotary positional embeddings, whose position-dependent rotations complicate the representation of the QK computation as a single composed operator. We therefore compose only the VO circuit (SLOA-VO), while merging 𝑾Q{\bm{W}}_{Q} and 𝑾K{\bm{W}}_{K} individually as linear operators. We evaluate both the original VO rank, ro​v=128r_{ov}{=}128, and expanded ranks, ro​v∈{256,384}r_{ov}\!\in\!\{256,384\}. Our comparisons include the baselines from §4.1 and the LoRA-specific baseline KnOTS-TIES (Stoica et al., 2025; Yadav et al., 2023). We evaluate math, code, and instruction-following performance on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), and IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023), respectively.

At the architecture-preserving rank ro​v=128r_{ov}{=}128, SLOA-VO achieves the highest average score among all merging methods, exceeding RegMean++ by 1.71.7 points. Increasing ro​vr_{ov} to 384384 further improves GSM8K and IFEval, with a small reduction in HumanEval performance (27.4427.44 versus 28.0528.05 at ro​v=128r_{ov}{=}128), indicating that the benefits of additional VO capacity vary across tasks. These results extend sequential operator alignment to LoRA experts on a 7B-parameter decoder-only model. Complementary experiments on LoRA-adapted ViT-B/32 experts, using both composed QK and VO operators, are presented in §F.2.

5 Related work

Data-free parameter-space merging. A broad class of data-free model merging methods considers task-specific models directly in parameter space. Uniform model soups average weights across models with the same architecture (Wortsman et al., 2022), while Task Arithmetic merges task vectors, defined as differences between fine-tuned and pretrained weights (Ilharco et al., 2023). Later methods reduce task interference: TIES-Merging removes small-magnitude updates and resolves sign conflicts (Yadav et al., 2023), DARE randomly drops and rescales task-vector entries (Yu et al., 2024), and spectral methods such as TSV-M and Iso-C/Iso-CTS manipulate the singular structure of task vectors to denoise or rescale merged updates (Gargiulo et al., 2025; Marczak et al., 2025). While attractive since they require no data or optimization, these methods merge parameter tensors instead of the computation units they implement. This is limiting in transformers, where attention depends on composed QK and OV operators and not isolated query, key, value, and output layers. SLOA instead merges these functional operators, removing dependence on arbitrary parameterizations.

Calibration-based training-free merging. Another line of work uses a small calibration set while still avoiding gradient-based training. Fisher Merging (Matena and Raffel, 2022) weights parameters according to their Fisher information, preserving parameters estimated to be important for the task losses. RegMean (Jin et al., 2023) solves a closed-form regression problem that aligns hidden representations of the merged model with those of the task-specific models. RegMean++ (Nguyen et al., 2026) improves this idea by computing statistics across layers, reducing the covariate shift caused by earlier merging errors. SLOA belongs to this training-free regime, but differs in the object being aligned. Prior methods mainly treat layers as independent units. In contrast, SLOA defines a local operator for each functional component: LayerNorm affine maps, linear maps, QK operators, and OV operators. This allows the same closed-form alignment principle to apply to both standard linear layers and coupled attention computations. Moreover, SLOA performs alignment sequentially under the activations produced by the partially merged model, so later operators are merged on the activations they will actually receive at inference time.

Test-time adaptation and training for merging. A separate class of methods improves merging by introducing learned coefficients, routers, task-specific components, or distillation objectives. AdaMerging (Yang et al., 2024b) learns layer-wise merging coefficients using unlabeled test samples. Twin-Merging (Lu et al., 2024) decomposes task vectors into shared and private components and uses a router to select fusion weights. EMR-Merging (Huang et al., 2024) maintains both shared and task-specific parameters, requiring task identity at inference time. Representation Surgery (Yang et al., 2024a) trains an auxiliary module to align representations, while ProDistill (Xu et al., 2025) formulates merging as a distillation problem with learned merging coefficients. These methods can achieve strong performance, but they require additional training, test-time data, task identity, routing, or teacher-student optimization. SLOA avoids these requirements: after collecting calibration activations, each local merge is solved in closed form, produces a single deployed model, and requires neither task identity nor test-time adaptation at inference time.

6 Conclusion

We presented Sequential Local Operator Alignment (SLOA), a training-free framework for merging transformers by aligning local functional operators. By treating the QK and VO products as the effective operators, matching each operator’s behavior under the partially merged model’s activations with a data-aware operator geometry, and merging sequentially in topological order, SLOA preserves task-specific behavior while reducing the growth of activation error across depth. The operator-level view also decouples the merged attention operator from its final factorization, making head rank an explicit capacity-control parameter. We evaluate SLOA on ViT-B/32 and ViT-B/16 with up to 20 tasks, RoBERTa on GLUE, LoRA-adapted ViT experts, and a VO-only variant for LoRA-adapted LLaMA-2-7B. Across these settings, SLOA outperforms strong merging baselines at the original head rank, showing that its gains do not require widening the deployed model. Its relative advantage becomes more pronounced as the number of merged tasks grows. Increasing the head rank can provide further gains beyond those obtained at the original rank.

One limitation of SLOA is that, like other calibration-based training-free methods, it requires a small unlabeled calibration set that represents each task’s input distribution. When such data are unavailable, data-free methods may be more suitable. In addition, SLOA follows a greedy sequential procedure. At each step, it optimizes a well-defined local objective, but it does not optimize a single end-to-end objective. Finally, SLOA requires more computation during merging than data-free methods and simpler calibration-based approaches because it propagates activations, solves local regression problems, and factorizes the merged operators. Increasing the rank beyond dkd_{k} also widens the attention heads, which increases inference time and memory use. Promising directions include reducing reliance on in-distribution calibration data through synthetic, generated, or proxy inputs, and combining SLOA with data free merging when calibration data provide insufficient coverage of some tasks. Extending the composed QK formulation to attention with relative or rotary position encodings would also broaden its architectural scope. Another direction is automatic per-head rank selection, allowing the merged model’s capacity to be allocated according to deployment constraints. More broadly, the proposed method supports a functional view of transformer merging: align local computations along the merged execution path, and choose the attention factorization to control how much of the aligned operators the deployed model retains for multi-task merging. In light of this view, the unit of merging does not need to be the unit of parameterization.

Appendix

Appendix A Additional background

A.1 Model Merging

Let there be a set of TT distinct tasks with corresponding training datasets 𝒟={D1,…,DT}\mathcal{D}=\{D_{1},\ldots,D_{T}\}. We assume a homogeneous neural network architecture parameterized by 𝚽∈ℝd\mathbf{\Phi}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, where dd denotes the total number of parameters. Let 𝚽pre∈ℝd\mathbf{\Phi}_{\text{pre}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the parameters of a large-scale pretrained foundation model (e.g., CLIP [Radford et al., 2021b]) that serves as a shared initialization. We are given TT task-specific models {𝚽1,…,𝚽T}\{\mathbf{\Phi}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{\Phi}_{T}\}, where each model 𝚽t\mathbf{\Phi}_{t} is obtained by independently fine-tuning 𝚽pre\mathbf{\Phi}_{\text{pre}} exclusively on its respective dataset DtD_{t}.

Model Merging. Model merging is the process of aggregating these distinct parameter sets into a single, unified multi-task model without requiring computationally expensive joint retraining on the original training datasets. Mathematically, we seek an aggregation function gg such that:

(8) 𝚽merge=g⁡(𝚽1,…,𝚽T).\mathbf{\Phi}_{\text{merge}}=g(\mathbf{\Phi}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{\Phi}_{T}).

Performance Objectives. The fundamental objective of model merging is to construct a single parameter set 𝚽merge\mathbf{\Phi}_{\text{merge}} that encapsulates the combined capabilities of all individual experts. Let ℳt:ℝd→ℝ\mathcal{M}_{t}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} denote a task-specific evaluation metric (e.g., accuracy) for task tt, where higher values indicate better performance. A successful merging function ensures that the unified model recovers the performance of the specialized experts:

(9) ℳt​(𝚽merge)≈ℳt​(𝚽t),∀t∈{1,…,T}.\mathcal{M}_{t}(\mathbf{\Phi}_{\text{merge}})\approx\mathcal{M}_{t}(\mathbf{\Phi}_{t}),\quad\forall t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}.

A.2 Transformer architecture and the attention operation

The Transformer architecture [Vaswani et al., 2017] has become the foundational backbone for state-of-the-art models across both vision and language domains. Structurally, a Transformer is composed of multiple identical, sequentially stacked layers For a given layer, the input representations are processed through two primary sub-modules: a (i) Multi-Head Attention (MHA) block and a (ii) Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), accompanied by Layer Normalization and residual connections.

Multi-Head Attention (MHA). The core of the Transformer is the attention mechanism, which routes information across sequence tokens. Let 𝑿∈ℝL×d{\bm{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} denote the input sequence of LL sequence length with model dimension dd. The matrices for the layer are defined as 𝑾Q,𝑾K,𝑾V,𝑾O∈ℝd×d{{\bm{W}}_{Q}},{{\bm{W}}_{K}},{{\bm{W}}_{V}},{{\bm{W}}_{O}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}.

To allow the model to jointly attend to information from different representations subspaces, the MHA operation divides the global matrices into HH independent heads. The global parameter matrices 𝑾Q,𝑾K,𝑾V,𝑾O∈ℝd×d{\bm{W}}_{Q},{\bm{W}}_{K},{\bm{W}}_{V},{\bm{W}}_{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} are partitioned across HH heads, where each head jj operates on a reduced subspace of dimension dk=d/Hd_{k}=d/H, with head-specific sub-matrices 𝑾Q(j),𝑾K(j),𝑾V(j)∈ℝd×dk{\bm{W}}_{Q}^{(j)},{\bm{W}}_{K}^{(j)},{\bm{W}}_{V}^{(j)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{k}} and 𝑾O(j)∈ℝdk×d{\bm{W}}_{O}^{(j)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times d} for the jj-th head. Crucially, instead of viewing MHA merely as a concatenation operation, it can be mathematically formulated as the sum of independent head contributions added directly to the residual stream. The output 𝒁MHA∈ℝn×d{\bm{Z}}_{\mathrm{MHA}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} of the MHA block is given by:

(10) 𝒁MHA=∑j=1Hsoftmax⁡((𝑿​𝑾Q(j))​(𝑿​𝑾K(j))⊤dk)​𝑿​𝑾V(j)​𝑾O(j){\bm{Z}}_{\mathrm{MHA}}=\sum_{j=1}^{H}\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{({\bm{X}}{\bm{W}}_{Q}^{(j)})({\bm{X}}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{(j)})^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right){\bm{X}}{\bm{W}}_{V}^{(j)}{\bm{W}}_{O}^{(j)}

This formulation highlights two distinct functional circuits within each head jj: the bilinear Query-Key (QK) circuit defined by 𝑾Q(j)​𝑾K(j)⊤{\bm{W}}_{Q}^{(j)}{{\bm{W}}_{K}^{(j)}}^{\top}, which determines attention scores, and the linear Value-Output (VO) circuit defined by 𝑾V(j)​𝑾O(j){\bm{W}}_{V}^{(j)}{\bm{W}}_{O}^{(j)}, which dictates the information written to the output [Elhage et al., 2021].

Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Following the attention mechanism, the representations pass through a two-layer MLP block. Let 𝑾1∈ℝd×do​u​t{\bm{W}}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{out}} and 𝑾2∈ℝdo​u​t×d{\bm{W}}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times d} be the first and the second MLP layer matrices, respectively. For an input representation to the MLP block, which we denote as 𝒁∈ℝL×d{\bm{Z}}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} (functionally the layer-normalized sum of 𝑿{\bm{X}} and 𝒁MHA{\bm{Z}}_{\mathrm{MHA}}), the block applies a non-linear activation function σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) (e.g., ReLU or GELU). The transformation sequence maps the inputs to the final block output 𝒁MLP∈ℝL×d{\bm{Z}}_{\mathrm{MLP}}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}: Algebraically, the operation of the entire MLP block is summarized as:

(11) 𝒁MLP=σ⁡(𝒁​𝑾1)​𝑾2{\bm{Z}}_{\mathrm{MLP}}=\sigma({\bm{Z}}{\bm{W}}_{1}){\bm{W}}_{2}

Appendix B Extended related work

B.1 Alignment under model symmetries and activation matching

Neural networks contain many parameter symmetries: different parameterizations can represent the same function [Dinh et al., 2017, Neyshabur et al., 2016, Zhao et al., 2025, Bona-Pellissier et al., 2023]. Prior work on model alignment and mode connectivity studies how to account for such symmetries before merging, for example by matching neurons, features, or permutations across independently trained networks [Ainsworth et al., 2023, Singh and Jaggi, 2020, Xu et al., 2024, Zhang et al., 2025]. These methods highlight an important principle: successful merging should compare models in a functionally meaningful coordinate system, rather than relying only on raw parameter coordinates.

Our work is motivated by the same non-identifiability issue, but addresses a different symmetry that appears inside transformer attention. For a single attention head, the transformation (𝑾Q,𝑾K)↦(𝑾Q​𝑹,𝑾K​𝑹−⁣⊤)({\bm{W}}_{Q},{\bm{W}}_{K})\mapsto({\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{R}},{\bm{W}}_{K}{\bm{R}}^{-\top}) leaves the QK operator 𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤{\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top} unchanged, and analogous changes of the value-head coordinates preserve the VO operator. Thus, aligning or averaging 𝑾Q{\bm{W}}_{Q}, 𝑾K{\bm{W}}_{K}, 𝑾V{\bm{W}}_{V}, and 𝑾O{\bm{W}}_{O} separately can break a computation that is shared at the operator level. Instead of first searching for a coordinate transformation between factorizations, SLOA removes this ambiguity by merging the invariant local operators themselves and factorizing the merged operators only after alignment.

B.2 Transformer circuits and operator structure

Several analyses of transformers emphasize that attention heads are naturally described through composed circuits rather than isolated projection matrices [Elhage et al., 2021, Dar et al., 2023, Vaswani et al., 2017, Theus et al., 2026]. In this view, the QK circuit controls the pre-softmax attention scores, while the VO, or OV, circuit controls how attended token representations are written back to the residual stream. This perspective has been influential for understanding transformer computation, but it has been less directly exploited in training-free model merging. SLOA turns this circuit-level view into a concrete merging algorithm. For each attention head, it constructs and aligns the QK and VO operators as residual-space maps. This also separates the operator being merged from the rank used to implement it. Each task-specific head realizes a low-rank operator because the head dimension is limited, but the merged multi-task operator can have higher effective rank when different tasks use different subspaces. SLOA therefore treats rank as a capacity-control mechanism: after solving for the merged ambient operator, it can either factorize it at the original head rank or retain additional singular directions through rank expansion. This differs from spectral task-vector methods, which apply SVD to task updates in weight space; in SLOA, the SVD is applied to the merged functional attention operator and determines how much of that operator is represented in the final head.

Appendix C Technical comparison to RegMean, RegMean++, rotation-symmetry matching, and ProDistill

C.1 Comparison with RegMean

We compare SLOA with Regression Mean (RegMean) [Jin et al., 2023]. RegMean is one of the closest predecessors to our method because it also derives a closed-form merging rule from a regression objective. However, RegMean and SLOA differ in the object being merged, the local objective being solved, the treatment of attention, and the role of calibration states.

RegMean as layer-wise linear regression.

Consider a linear layer whose local behavior in task model tt is

(12) 𝑿t​𝑾t,{\bm{X}}_{t}{\bm{W}}_{t},

where 𝑿t{\bm{X}}_{t} denotes the input activations to that linear layer and 𝑾t{\bm{W}}_{t} is the corresponding task-specific weight matrix. RegMean seeks a merged weight 𝑾{\bm{W}} whose outputs match the outputs of the individual task layers on their own layer inputs:

(13) min⁡∑t=1T𝑾⁡‖𝑿t​𝑾−𝑿t​𝑾t‖F2.\min_{{\bm{W}}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|{\bm{X}}_{t}{\bm{W}}-{\bm{X}}_{t}{\bm{W}}_{t}\right\|_{F}^{2}.

Let

(14) 𝑮t=𝑿t⊤​𝑿t{\bm{G}}_{t}={\bm{X}}_{t}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{t}

be the input Gram matrix for task model tt. The closed-form RegMean solution is

(15) 𝑾RegMean=(∑t=1T𝑮t)−1​(∑t=1T𝑮t​𝑾t),{\bm{W}}_{\mathrm{RegMean}}=\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\bm{G}}_{t}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\bm{G}}_{t}{\bm{W}}_{t}\right),

up to the normalization convention used for the empirical average. In transformer models, RegMean applies this rule independently to each linear layer. Other parameters, such as embeddings, biases, and normalization parameters, are typically merged by simple averaging.

Connection to SLOA for ordinary linear maps.

SLOA reduces to a RegMean-like objective in a restricted special case. For an ordinary one-sided linear map, SLOA uses the local behavior map

(16) 𝒜⁡(𝑿,𝑾)=𝑿​𝑾.\mathcal{A}({\bm{X}};{\bm{W}})={\bm{X}}{\bm{W}}.

If we ignore the sequential activation mismatch by setting

(17) 𝑿^t,i=𝑿t,i\widehat{{\bm{X}}}_{t,i}={\bm{X}}_{t,i}

for all calibration examples, and if we remove the additional operator-geometry regularizer, then the SLOA activation-matching term becomes

(18) min𝑾∑t=1T∑i=1nt‖𝑿t,i𝑾−𝑿t,i𝑾t‖F2,\min_{{\bm{W}}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\left\|{\bm{X}}_{t,i}{\bm{W}}-{\bm{X}}_{t,i}{\bm{W}}_{t}\right\|_{F}^{2},

which is exactly the RegMean regression problem for linear layers. Thus, RegMean can be viewed as a special case of local behavior matching for isolated one-sided linear operators under task-model activations.

The purpose of SLOA is to go beyond this special case. SLOA changes both the local inputs and the operator space:

(19) 𝒜⁡(𝒁^t,i,𝜽)≈𝒜⁡(𝒁t,i,𝜽t),\mathcal{A}\left(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta}\right)\approx\mathcal{A}\left({\bm{Z}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta}_{t}\right),

where 𝒁^t,i\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i} is produced by the partially merged model and 𝒁t,i{\bm{Z}}_{t,i} is produced by the original task model. For linear maps, this gives an objective of the form

(20) min⁡∑t=1T𝑾⁡‖𝑿^t​𝑾−𝑿t​𝑾t‖F2+∑t=1T‖𝑾−𝑾t‖χ^t2.\min_{{\bm{W}}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|\widehat{{\bm{X}}}_{t}{\bm{W}}-{\bm{X}}_{t}{\bm{W}}_{t}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|{\bm{W}}-{\bm{W}}_{t}\right\|_{\widehat{\chi}_{t}}^{2}.

The corresponding normal equations involve both the partially merged Gram matrix

(21) 𝑿^t⊤​𝑿^t\widehat{{\bm{X}}}_{t}^{\top}\widehat{{\bm{X}}}_{t}

and the cross-state term

(22) 𝑿^t⊤​𝑿t​𝑾t.\widehat{{\bm{X}}}_{t}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{t}{\bm{W}}_{t}.

This is different from RegMean, whose objective uses the same task-model input 𝑿t{\bm{X}}_{t} on both sides of the regression.

Independent linear-layer merging versus local functional operators.

The main limitation of RegMean from our perspective is that it treats each linear layer as the primitive unit of merging. This is appropriate for genuinely one-sided linear maps, but it is not aligned with the computation inside transformer attention. In a transformer head, the query and key weights do not determine attention scores independently. Rather, the pre-softmax attention scores depend on the composed operator

(23) 𝜽Q​K,t(j)=𝑾Q,t(j)​(𝑾K,t(j))⊤dk.\bm{\theta}_{QK,t}^{(j)}=\frac{{\bm{W}}_{Q,t}^{(j)}\big({\bm{W}}_{K,t}^{(j)}\big)^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}.

Similarly, the value and output weights determine the residual write map through

(24) 𝜽V​O,t(j)=𝑾V,t(j)​𝑾O,t(j).\bm{\theta}_{VO,t}^{(j)}={\bm{W}}_{V,t}^{(j)}{\bm{W}}_{O,t}^{(j)}.

RegMean applies regression to the individual projection matrices, treating 𝑾Q{\bm{W}}_{Q}, 𝑾K{\bm{W}}_{K}, 𝑾V{\bm{W}}_{V}, and 𝑾O{\bm{W}}_{O} as separate linear maps. SLOA instead treats 𝜽Q​K\bm{\theta}_{QK} and 𝜽V​O\bm{\theta}_{VO} as the local functional operators to be merged.

This distinction matters because the individual attention factors are not identifiable from the attention computation. For any invertible matrix 𝑹{\bm{R}},

(25) 𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤=(𝑾Q​𝑹)​(𝑾K​𝑹−⁣⊤)⊤.{\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top}=({\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{R}})({\bm{W}}_{K}{\bm{R}}^{-\top})^{\top}.

Thus, two models can have the same QK score operator but different query/key coordinates. A method that merges 𝑾Q{\bm{W}}_{Q} and 𝑾K{\bm{W}}_{K} independently is sensitive to this arbitrary factorization. SLOA removes this ambiguity by merging the composed QK operator directly. The same argument applies to the VO circuit.

One-sided geometry versus two-sided attention geometry.

RegMean uses input Gram matrices for one-sided linear maps. For a linear map 𝑿​𝑾{\bm{X}}{\bm{W}}, this is natural because the local discrepancy is measured after left multiplication by 𝑿{\bm{X}}. However, the QK behavior map is not one-sided:

(26) 𝒜⁡(𝑿,𝜽Q​K)=𝑿​𝜽Q​K​𝑿⊤.\mathcal{A}({\bm{X}};\bm{\theta}_{QK})={\bm{X}}\bm{\theta}_{QK}{\bm{X}}^{\top}.

SLOA therefore uses a two-sided metric for QK operators:

(27) ‖𝜽−𝜽t‖χ^t2=‖𝚲t1/2​(𝜽−𝜽t)​𝚲t1/2‖F2,\left\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\|_{\widehat{\chi}_{t}}^{2}=\left\|{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}^{1/2}(\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t}){\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}^{1/2}\right\|_{F}^{2},

which corresponds after vectorization to a Mahalanobis metric with covariance structure

(28) 𝚲t⊗𝚲t.{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\otimes{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}.

This two-sided geometry has no analogue in RegMean because RegMean does not formulate QK as a bilinear residual-space operator.

Dataless statistics versus sequential calibration states.

RegMean was designed for a dataless knowledge-fusion setting: the model provider can release the fine-tuned weights together with low-dimensional inner-product statistics, without sharing the original training data. This is an important privacy and deployment advantage. SLOA instead targets the training-free calibration-data setting. It uses a small calibration set to run both the task models and the partially merged model, collecting the states required for local behavior matching and data-dependent operator regularization. Since SLOA evaluates each local operator on the states produced by the partially merged model, it can correct for upstream merging errors. RegMean computes each layer’s merge from the task-model layer inputs and therefore implicitly assumes that previous merged layers will reproduce the task-model activations accurately. SLOA does not make this assumption: the merged operator is evaluated on the activation distribution it will actually receive during the merged model’s forward pass.

Rank and capacity.

RegMean preserves the original architecture because it directly solves for each original weight matrix. For attention, this means the head dimension remains fixed and the rank of each QK or VO product remains constrained by the original factorization. SLOA decouples the merged operator from its final factorization. It first solves for the merged QK or VO operator in the ambient residual-space operator space

(29) Θamb=ℝd×d,\Theta_{\mathrm{amb}}=\mathbb{R}^{d\times d},

and only afterward factorizes the operator at a chosen rank rr. This allows either rank-preserving merging with r=dkr=d_{k} or rank-expanded merging with r>dkr>d_{k}. RegMean does not expose this rank-control mechanism because it never explicitly constructs the composed attention operator.

C.2 Comparison with RegMean++

We next compare SLOA with RegMean++ [Nguyen et al., 2026]. RegMean++ identifies an important limitation of RegMean: independently merging each linear layer using task-model activations ignores the way representation errors propagate through the merged network. RegMean++ addresses this by recomputing statistics progressively using activations produced by previously merged layers. SLOA shares this sequential motivation, but differs in the local objective, the treatment of attention, the operator geometry, and the final factorization step.

RegMean++ as progressive RegMean.

RegMean++ keeps the core RegMean closed-form linear-layer solve. The key modification is how the layer statistics are collected. In RegMean, the input statistics for a layer are obtained from the corresponding task model. In RegMean++, the current layer is processed after earlier layers have already been merged, so the statistics for later layers are computed using activations induced by the partially merged model. This makes the regression statistics more consistent with the actual feature distribution that the merged model will experience.

Schematically, let 𝑯t(ℓ−1){\bm{H}}_{t}^{(\ell-1)} denote the activation entering transformer layer ℓ\ell for task tt. RegMean uses the task-model state

(30) 𝑯t(ℓ−1)=ft(<ℓ)​(𝑿t),{\bm{H}}_{t}^{(\ell-1)}=f_{t}^{(<\ell)}({\bm{X}}_{t}),

whereas RegMean++ uses a merged-model state of the form

(31) 𝑯^t(ℓ−1)=fmerge(<ℓ)​(𝑿t).\widehat{{\bm{H}}}_{t}^{(\ell-1)}=f_{\mathrm{merge}}^{(<\ell)}({\bm{X}}_{t}).

The resulting statistics are then used in the same RegMean-style closed-form solve for the linear layers inside the current transformer layer. Thus, RegMean++ is progressive in the sense that earlier merged layers influence the feature statistics used to merge later layers.

Shared motivation with SLOA.

SLOA agrees with the core diagnosis of RegMean++: a layer should not be merged under the assumption that all preceding layers have been merged perfectly. If earlier merges shift the hidden states, then later layers should be aligned under the shifted hidden states that the final merged model will actually produce. This is exactly why SLOA introduces the partially merged local input 𝒁^t,i(m)\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{(m)} for operator omo_{m}.

However, SLOA uses this sequential state in a different regression problem. At operator omo_{m}, SLOA solves

(32) 𝒜⁡(𝒁^t,i(m),𝜽)≈𝒜⁡(𝒁t,i(m),𝜽t(m)),\mathcal{A}\left(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{(m)};\bm{\theta}\right)\approx\mathcal{A}\left({\bm{Z}}_{t,i}^{(m)};\bm{\theta}_{t}^{(m)}\right),

where 𝒁^t,i(m)\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{(m)} is the state seen by the partially merged model and 𝒁t,i(m){\bm{Z}}_{t,i}^{(m)} is the state seen by the original task model. Thus, the merged operator is trained to act on the actual merged-model input while matching the task-model local behavior (i.e., output). This creates a corrective objective that explicitly bridges the shifted merged-model state and the task-model target behavior.

Progressive statistics versus corrective local behavior matching.

RegMean++ modifies RegMean by making the statistics progressive. SLOA modifies the objective itself. For an ordinary linear map, SLOA uses

(33) min⁡∑t=1T𝑾⁡‖𝑿^t​𝑾−𝑿t​𝑾t‖F2+∑t=1T‖𝑾−𝑾t‖χ^t2.\min_{{\bm{W}}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|\widehat{{\bm{X}}}_{t}{\bm{W}}-{\bm{X}}_{t}{\bm{W}}_{t}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|{\bm{W}}-{\bm{W}}_{t}\right\|_{\widehat{\chi}_{t}}^{2}.

The left side of the behavior-matching term uses the partially merged input 𝑿^t\widehat{{\bm{X}}}_{t}, while the target output uses the original task-model behavior 𝑿t​𝑾t{\bm{X}}_{t}{\bm{W}}_{t}. Consequently, the closed-form solution depends not only on a merged-model Gram matrix

(34) 𝑿^t⊤​𝑿^t,\widehat{{\bm{X}}}_{t}^{\top}\widehat{{\bm{X}}}_{t},

but also on a cross-state term

(35) 𝑿^t⊤​𝑿t​𝑾t.\widehat{{\bm{X}}}_{t}^{\top}{\bm{X}}_{t}{\bm{W}}_{t}.

This cross-state term directly compensates for the mismatch between the state that the merged model receives and the state under which the task-specific operator was originally used.

RegMean++ instead keeps the RegMean form of the linear-layer solve, but obtains the features progressively from the merged computation. This improves over RegMean by incorporating cross-layer dependencies, but it still treats the current component as an isolated linear layer whose input statistics are updated. SLOA uses the progressive state as part of a local functional matching problem between two execution paths.

Layer-wise progression versus operator-wise topological progression.

RegMean++ progresses at the transformer-layer level. Within a transformer layer, it computes statistics for linear layers and merges those linear weights using the RegMean rule. Other parameters, including non-linear or normalization parameters, are merged by averaging.

SLOA progresses at the level of local operators in a topological order. The local operators include LayerNorm affine maps, ordinary linear maps, QK attention operators, and VO attention operators. This finer granularity matters inside a transformer block because the internal attention computations have distinct functional roles: QK controls token routing through attention scores, whereas VO controls the residual write map after attention aggregation. A layer-wise regression method can update statistics progressively, but it does not explicitly represent these two coupled attention mechanisms as separate functional operators. SLOA does.

Treatment of attention.

The most important difference is the treatment of self-attention. RegMean++ inherits RegMean’s parameterization and applies regression to linear projection matrices. Thus, the attention projections are still treated as individual linear maps. This means that the query, key, value, and output matrices are merged as parameter tensors rather than as the composed operators that determine attention behavior.

SLOA instead defines the QK and VO local operators as

(36) 𝜽Q​K,t(j)=𝑾Q,t(j)​(𝑾K,t(j))⊤dk,𝜽V​O,t(j)=𝑾V,t(j)​𝑾O,t(j).\bm{\theta}_{QK,t}^{(j)}=\frac{{\bm{W}}_{Q,t}^{(j)}\big({\bm{W}}_{K,t}^{(j)}\big)^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}},\qquad\bm{\theta}_{VO,t}^{(j)}={\bm{W}}_{V,t}^{(j)}{\bm{W}}_{O,t}^{(j)}.

These are the objects that determine the pre-softmax attention scores and the residual write map, respectively. Therefore, SLOA aligns attention at the level of local function rather than at the level of arbitrary attention-coordinate factors.

For any invertible matrix 𝑹{\bm{R}},

(37) 𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤=(𝑾Q​𝑹)​(𝑾K​𝑹−⁣⊤)⊤.{\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top}=({\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{R}})({\bm{W}}_{K}{\bm{R}}^{-\top})^{\top}.

Thus, two QK factorizations can be functionally identical while their individual query and key matrices differ. RegMean++ can reduce covariate shift through progressive statistics, but it does not remove this factorization ambiguity because it still merges the individual factors. SLOA removes the ambiguity by merging the invariant composed operator.

Operator geometry.

RegMean++ uses RegMean-style Gram statistics for linear layers. This remains a one-sided geometry appropriate for maps of the form

(38) 𝑿​𝑾.{\bm{X}}{\bm{W}}.

SLOA uses different geometries for different local operators. For one-sided operators, such as linear maps and VO, SLOA uses a Mahalanobis geometry induced by the calibration activations:

(39) ‖𝜽−𝜽t‖χ^t2=Tr⁡[(𝜽−𝜽t)⊤​𝚲t​(𝜽−𝜽t)].\left\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\|_{\widehat{\chi}_{t}}^{2}=\operatorname{Tr}\left[(\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t})^{\top}{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}(\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t})\right].

For QK, whose behavior is bilinear in the residual state,

(40) 𝒜⁡(𝑿,𝜽Q​K)=𝑿​𝜽Q​K​𝑿⊤,\mathcal{A}({\bm{X}};\bm{\theta}_{QK})={\bm{X}}\bm{\theta}_{QK}{\bm{X}}^{\top},

SLOA uses the two-sided metric

(41) ‖𝜽−𝜽t‖χ^t2=‖𝚲t1/2​(𝜽−𝜽t)​𝚲t1/2‖F2.\left\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\|_{\widehat{\chi}_{t}}^{2}=\left\|{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}^{1/2}(\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t}){\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}^{1/2}\right\|_{F}^{2}.

This operator-specific geometry is absent from RegMean++, because RegMean++ does not formulate QK as a two-sided residual-space operator.

LayerNorm and non-linear components.

RegMean++ improves the statistics used for linear-layer merging, but it still handles non-linear and normalization-related parameters by simple averaging. SLOA includes LayerNorm affine parameters in the same local-operator alignment framework. After the normalization statistics are fixed for a given input, the LayerNorm affine map is linear in (𝜸,𝜷)(\bm{\gamma},\bm{\beta}):

(42) 𝒜⁡(𝑿,𝜸,𝜷)=ν⁡(𝑿)​diag⁡(𝜸)+𝟏​𝜷⊤.\mathcal{A}({\bm{X}};\bm{\gamma},\bm{\beta})=\nu({\bm{X}})\operatorname{diag}(\bm{\gamma})+\mathbf{1}\bm{\beta}^{\top}.

Therefore, SLOA can align LayerNorm behavior with a closed-form local objective instead of simply averaging the affine parameters. This is useful because LayerNorm parameters affect the scale and shift of the states that downstream operators receive.

Rank and capacity control.

RegMean++ preserves the original architecture. Since it merges existing attention projection matrices, the attention head dimension remains fixed at dkd_{k}. The method therefore does not expose the spectrum of the merged QK or VO operator and cannot choose how much rank to retain after merging.

SLOA explicitly separates the merged operator from its factorization. After solving for an ambient QK or VO operator

(43) 𝜽¯(j)∈ℝd×d,\bar{\bm{\theta}}^{(j)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d},

SLOA factorizes it at a chosen rank rjr_{j}. When rj=dkr_{j}=d_{k}, the original head dimension is preserved. When rj>dkr_{j}>d_{k}, the merged model can retain additional singular directions that arise from combining task-specific low-rank operators. This provides a capacity-control mechanism that is not available to RegMean++.

Different notions of “sequential”.

Both RegMean++ and SLOA are sequential, but the sequentiality serves different purposes.

RegMean++ is sequential because the statistics used for later layers are recomputed from activations influenced by earlier merged layers. Its main goal is to make RegMean’s input statistics more faithful to the merged model’s internal feature distribution.

SLOA is sequential because each local operator is aligned under the actual execution path of the partially merged model. The target remains the task-specific local behavior, while the input to the merged operator is the partially merged input. Thus, each local solve is not only statistics-aware but also corrective:

(44) merged operator on merged state≈task operator on task state.\text{merged operator on merged state}\quad\approx\quad\text{task operator on task state}.

SLOA’s cross-state matching explicitly accounts for that shift.

C.3 Comparison with rotation-symmetry matching

We provide a detailed comparison with weight space rotation-symmetry matching [Zhang et al., 2025]. This work is closely related to ours because it also recognizes that transformer attention contains nontrivial symmetries beyond permutation symmetry. However, the two methods use this observation in fundamentally different ways. Rotation-symmetry matching searches for functionally equivalent parameterizations of the input models that are closer in weight space before applying a conventional model-fusion rule. SLOA instead changes the object being merged: it constructs, aligns, and merges the local functional operators themselves.

Rotation-symmetry matching.

[Zhang et al., 2025] observe that the self-attention factors are not individually identifiable. For a single attention head, if 𝑹{\bm{R}} is an orthogonal matrix, then the transformation

(45) 𝑾Q↦𝑾Q​𝑹,𝑾K↦𝑾K​𝑹{\bm{W}}_{Q}\mapsto{\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{R}},\qquad{\bm{W}}_{K}\mapsto{\bm{W}}_{K}{\bm{R}}

preserves the QK score operator because

(46) (𝑾Q​𝑹)​(𝑾K​𝑹)⊤=𝑾Q​𝑹​𝑹⊤​𝑾K⊤=𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤.({\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{R}})({\bm{W}}_{K}{\bm{R}})^{\top}={\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{R}}{\bm{R}}^{\top}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top}={\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top}.

Similarly, for the value-output path, the transformation

(47) 𝑾V↦𝑾V​𝑺,𝑾O↦𝑺⊤​𝑾O,{\bm{W}}_{V}\mapsto{\bm{W}}_{V}{\bm{S}},\qquad{\bm{W}}_{O}\mapsto{\bm{S}}^{\top}{\bm{W}}_{O},

with orthogonal 𝑺{\bm{S}}, preserves the VO operator:

(48) (𝑾V​𝑺)​(𝑺⊤​𝑾O)=𝑾V​𝑾O.({\bm{W}}_{V}{\bm{S}})({\bm{S}}^{\top}{\bm{W}}_{O})={\bm{W}}_{V}{\bm{W}}_{O}.

Based on these invariances, rotation-symmetry matching chooses rotations that make one model’s attention parameters close to another model’s attention parameters in Euclidean distance. For example, in the QK case, the matching problem can be viewed as an orthogonal Procrustes-type objective of the form

(49) min𝑹⊤​𝑹=𝑰⁡‖𝑾Q,1​𝑹−𝑾Q,2‖F2+‖𝑾K,1​𝑹−𝑾K,2‖F2,\min_{{\bm{R}}^{\top}{\bm{R}}={\bm{I}}}\left\|{\bm{W}}_{Q,1}{\bm{R}}-{\bm{W}}_{Q,2}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\left\|{\bm{W}}_{K,1}{\bm{R}}-{\bm{W}}_{K,2}\right\|_{F}^{2},

with an analogous objective for the VO factors. After this matching step, the transformed models are merged using an existing fusion method, such as weight averaging, Fisher merging, or RegMean. Thus, rotation-symmetry matching is a preprocessing or re-basing step for parameter-space fusion.

SLOA merges operators, not matched parameter factors.

SLOA starts from the same structural fact that QK and VO factors are not individually meaningful. However, rather than searching for rotations that make the factors close in parameter space, SLOA eliminates the factorization ambiguity by directly forming the composed operators

(50) 𝜽Q​K,t(j)=𝑾Q,t(j)​(𝑾K,t(j))⊤dk,𝜽V​O,t(j)=𝑾V,t(j)​𝑾O,t(j).\bm{\theta}_{QK,t}^{(j)}=\frac{{\bm{W}}_{Q,t}^{(j)}\big({\bm{W}}_{K,t}^{(j)}\big)^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}},\qquad\bm{\theta}_{VO,t}^{(j)}={\bm{W}}_{V,t}^{(j)}{\bm{W}}_{O,t}^{(j)}.

The optimization variable in SLOA is the operator 𝜽\bm{\theta} itself, not a rotation matrix and not the individual factors. For each local operator, SLOA solves

(51) 𝜽merge=arg⁡min𝜽∈Θamb​ℒact​(𝜽)+1T​∑t=1T‖𝜽−𝜽t‖χ^t2.\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}=\underset{\bm{\theta}\in\Theta_{\mathrm{amb}}}{\arg\min}\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}(\bm{\theta})+\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\|_{\widehat{\chi}_{t}}^{2}.

The merged operator is then factorized back into attention-compatible weights. Thus, the order of operations is different and this difference is central. Rotation matching preserves the function of each individual model before fusion, but the final fused model is still produced by merging the individual parameter factors. SLOA instead performs the merge in the space of the functional objects that determine the local computation.

Why factor matching does not remove factor-level interference.

Even after rotation matching, factor-wise merging can introduce cross terms that are not determined by the desired QK or VO operators. Consider two QK heads, and suppose model 11 has been rotation-matched to model 22 using an orthogonal matrix 𝑹{\bm{R}}. If we then average the matched factors,

(52) 𝑾¯Q=12​(𝑾Q,1​𝑹+𝑾Q,2),𝑾¯K=12​(𝑾K,1​𝑹+𝑾K,2),\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{Q}=\frac{1}{2}\left({\bm{W}}_{Q,1}{\bm{R}}+{\bm{W}}_{Q,2}\right),\qquad\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{K}=\frac{1}{2}\left({\bm{W}}_{K,1}{\bm{R}}+{\bm{W}}_{K,2}\right),

then the resulting QK operator is

𝑾¯Q​𝑾¯K⊤=14​(CLOSE\displaystyle\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{Q}\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{K}^{\top}=\frac{1}{4}\Big( OPEN𝑾Q,1​𝑾K,1⊤+𝑾Q,2​𝑾K,2⊤+𝑾Q,1​𝑹​𝑾K,2⊤+𝑾Q,2​𝑹⊤​𝑾K,1⊤).\displaystyle{\bm{W}}_{Q,1}{\bm{W}}_{K,1}^{\top}+{\bm{W}}_{Q,2}{\bm{W}}_{K,2}^{\top}+{\bm{W}}_{Q,1}{\bm{R}}{\bm{W}}_{K,2}^{\top}+{\bm{W}}_{Q,2}{\bm{R}}^{\top}{\bm{W}}_{K,1}^{\top}\Big).

The first two terms are the task-specific QK operators. The last two terms are cross terms that depend on the particular factorization and the chosen rotation. They are not functions only of the task operators 𝑾Q,1​𝑾K,1⊤{\bm{W}}_{Q,1}{\bm{W}}_{K,1}^{\top} and 𝑾Q,2​𝑾K,2⊤{\bm{W}}_{Q,2}{\bm{W}}_{K,2}^{\top}. Thus, even if the rotation makes the factors closer, the final factor-wise average is not the same as an operator-level merge.

The same issue appears for VO. After matching model 11 with an orthogonal matrix 𝑺{\bm{S}}, factor averaging gives

(53) 𝑾¯V=12​(𝑾V,1​𝑺+𝑾V,2),𝑾¯O=12​(𝑺⊤​𝑾O,1+𝑾O,2),\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{V}=\frac{1}{2}\left({\bm{W}}_{V,1}{\bm{S}}+{\bm{W}}_{V,2}\right),\qquad\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{O}=\frac{1}{2}\left({\bm{S}}^{\top}{\bm{W}}_{O,1}+{\bm{W}}_{O,2}\right),

and therefore

𝑾¯V​𝑾¯O=14​(CLOSE\displaystyle\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{V}\bar{{\bm{W}}}_{O}=\frac{1}{4}\Big( OPEN𝑾V,1​𝑾O,1+𝑾V,2​𝑾O,2+𝑾V,1​𝑺​𝑾O,2+𝑾V,2​𝑺⊤​𝑾O,1).\displaystyle{\bm{W}}_{V,1}{\bm{W}}_{O,1}+{\bm{W}}_{V,2}{\bm{W}}_{O,2}+{\bm{W}}_{V,1}{\bm{S}}{\bm{W}}_{O,2}+{\bm{W}}_{V,2}{\bm{S}}^{\top}{\bm{W}}_{O,1}\Big).

Again, the cross terms are artifacts of merging the factors rather than the composed VO operators. SLOA avoids this issue by solving directly for the merged QK and VO operators.

Different invariance classes.

Rotation-symmetry matching works within an orthogonal symmetry class, optionally combined with scalar rescaling. This is natural for parameter matching because orthogonal transformations preserve Frobenius norms and lead to efficient Procrustes-style solutions. However, the functional non-identifiability of QK and VO operators is larger. For any invertible matrix 𝑹{\bm{R}}, the QK product is preserved by

(54) 𝑾Q↦𝑾Q​𝑹,𝑾K↦𝑾K​𝑹−⁣⊤,{\bm{W}}_{Q}\mapsto{\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{R}},\qquad{\bm{W}}_{K}\mapsto{\bm{W}}_{K}{\bm{R}}^{-\top},

since

(55) (𝑾Q​𝑹)​(𝑾K​𝑹−⁣⊤)⊤=𝑾Q​𝑹​𝑹−1​𝑾K⊤=𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤.({\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{R}})({\bm{W}}_{K}{\bm{R}}^{-\top})^{\top}={\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{R}}{\bm{R}}^{-1}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top}={\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top}.

Similarly, the VO product is invariant under

(56) 𝑾V↦𝑾V​𝑹,𝑾O↦𝑹−1​𝑾O.{\bm{W}}_{V}\mapsto{\bm{W}}_{V}{\bm{R}},\qquad{\bm{W}}_{O}\mapsto{\bm{R}}^{-1}{\bm{W}}_{O}.

SLOA is invariant to this full product-level ambiguity because it only depends on the composed operator. If two factorizations realize the same QK or VO operator, they become exactly the same object for SLOA. By contrast, rotation matching selects a representative within a restricted symmetry family and then still applies a parameter-space fusion rule.

Different objectives.

The optimality guarantees of the two methods are for different problems. Rotation-symmetry matching is optimal for choosing an equivalent parameterization that minimizes Euclidean distance to an anchor model under orthogonal rotation constraints. Its objective is parameter proximity, where it chooses an equivalent representative that is close in weight space. This is useful because many model-fusion methods perform better when the input models are close in parameter space.

SLOA’s closed-form solution is optimal for a local data-aware operator-alignment objective. Its objective is local functional agreement:

(57) 𝒜⁡(𝒁^t,i,𝜽)≈𝒜⁡(𝒁t,i,𝜽t),\mathcal{A}\left(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta}\right)\approx\mathcal{A}\left({\bm{Z}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta}_{t}\right),

together with a data-dependent operator-space regularizer. Thus, SLOA does not ask for the closest equivalent factorization of a task model. It asks for the merged local operator that best reproduces the task-specific local behaviors under the activations that the partially merged model will actually produce.

Sequential correction versus independent parameter matching.

Rotation-symmetry matching is applied as a matching step between model parameters, typically module by module or layer by layer. The matching transformation preserves the function of the source model before fusion, but it does not explicitly account for the activation distribution induced by earlier merged components.

SLOA is sequential in a different sense. At operator omo_{m}, it evaluates the merged operator on the local input 𝒁^t,i(m)\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{(m)} produced by the partially merged model, while the target is the output of the task-specific operator on the task-model local input 𝒁t,i(m){\bm{Z}}_{t,i}^{(m)}:

(58) 𝒜⁡(𝒁^t,i(m),𝜽)≈𝒜⁡(𝒁t,i(m),𝜽t(m)).\mathcal{A}\left(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{(m)};\bm{\theta}\right)\approx\mathcal{A}\left({\bm{Z}}_{t,i}^{(m)};\bm{\theta}_{t}^{(m)}\right).

This makes each local merge corrective with respect to upstream merging errors. The method therefore aligns operators under the actual execution path of the merged network, rather than only reducing parameter distance between the original task models.

Anchor-based matching versus symmetric multi-model alignment.

The core rotation-matching formulation aligns one source model to an anchor model. For multi-model fusion, this requires choosing an anchor or performing matching relative to some reference representation. This anchor choice is natural for parameter matching, but it introduces an asymmetry among the input models.

SLOA treats all task models symmetrically in the local objective:

(59) 1T​∑t=1T1nt​∑i=1nt‖𝒜⁡(𝒁^t,i,𝜽)−𝒜⁡(𝒁t,i,𝜽t)‖F2.\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\left\|\mathcal{A}\left(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta}\right)-\mathcal{A}\left({\bm{Z}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta}_{t}\right)\right\|_{F}^{2}.

No single task model serves as the canonical parameter reference. The merged operator is estimated from a balanced objective over all task-specific operators and calibration states.

Rank and capacity control.

Rotation-symmetry matching preserves the original architecture during matching and subsequent fusion. In particular, the attention head dimension remains fixed, and the matched QK and VO products remain represented through the original head bottleneck.

SLOA decouples the merged operator from its factorization rank. The aligned QK and VO operators are first solved in the ambient residual-space operator space ℝd×d\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. Only after the operator is obtained do we choose a factorization rank rr. When r=dkr=d_{k}, the original head dimension is preserved. When r>dkr>d_{k}, SLOA can retain additional singular directions of the merged operator that arise from combining multiple task-specific subspaces. This rank-expansion mechanism has no analogue in rotation-symmetry matching, because rotation matching modifies existing factors but does not expose or refactorize the merged operator spectrum.

Data usage and scope.

Rotation-symmetry matching is primarily data-free: the matching transformation is computed from model parameters and can be plugged into several downstream fusion rules. This is an advantage when calibration data are unavailable. SLOA uses calibration data and therefore targets the training-free, data-aware setting. The calibration data serve two roles: they define the local behavior-matching targets and they induce the data-dependent operator metric used for regularization. Thus, SLOA trades the data-free nature of rotation matching for a more functional, data-aware merge.

Complementarity.

The two methods should be viewed as complementary rather than redundant. Rotation-symmetry matching shows that transformer attention has useful continuous parameter-space symmetries and that exploiting these symmetries can improve conventional model fusion. SLOA takes the next step from symmetry-aware factor matching to symmetry-invariant operator merging. Instead of choosing better representatives within the equivalence class and then merging factors, SLOA quotients out the factorization ambiguity by working directly with the composed QK and VO operators.

C.4 Comparison to ProDistill

We provide a detailed comparison between SLOA and ProDistill [Xu et al., 2025], as both methods use calibration data and proceed progressively through the network. Despite this superficial similarity, the two methods address different merging problems and optimize fundamentally different objects.

Overview of ProDistill.

ProDistill views model merging as a multi-teacher distillation problem. Let 𝜽0\bm{\theta}_{0} be the pretrained initialization and let 𝜽t\bm{\theta}_{t} be the fine-tuned model for task tt. Writing the task vector as 𝝉t=𝜽t−𝜽0,\bm{\tau}_{t}=\bm{\theta}_{t}-\bm{\theta}_{0}, ProDistill parameterizes the merged model as

(60) 𝜽^=𝜽0+∑t=1T𝝀t∘𝝉t,\widehat{\bm{\theta}}=\bm{\theta}_{0}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bm{\lambda}_{t}\circ\bm{\tau}_{t},

where 𝝀t\bm{\lambda}_{t} are learned merging coefficients and ∘\circ denotes element-wise multiplication. The method optimizes these coefficients so that the intermediate representations of the merged model match those of the fine-tuned teacher models on a small unlabeled validation set.

To reduce memory cost, ProDistill decomposes the objective layer by layer. At layer ℓ\ell, it solves an optimization problem of the form

(61) min⁡∑t=1T{𝝀t(ℓ)}t=1T⁡1|Dt|​∑(z1,z2)∈Dt(ℓ−1)‖ϕ(ℓ)​(𝜽0(ℓ)+∑s=1T𝝀s(ℓ)∘𝝉s(ℓ),z1)−ϕ(ℓ)​(𝜽t(ℓ),z2)‖22,\min_{\{\bm{\lambda}^{(\ell)}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{1}{|D_{t}|}\sum_{(z_{1},z_{2})\in D_{t}^{(\ell-1)}}\left\|\phi^{(\ell)}\left(\bm{\theta}_{0}^{(\ell)}+\sum_{s=1}^{T}\bm{\lambda}^{(\ell)}_{s}\circ\bm{\tau}^{(\ell)}_{s},z_{1}\right)-\phi^{(\ell)}\left(\bm{\theta}^{(\ell)}_{t},z_{2}\right)\right\|_{2}^{2},

where z1z_{1} is the input activation produced by the partially merged model and z2z_{2} is the corresponding input activation produced by the fine-tuned model. After optimizing the coefficients for layer ℓ\ell, ProDistill updates the paired activations and proceeds to the next layer. Thus, ProDistill is a progressive activation-distillation method over task-vector coefficients.

SLOA is training-free, whereas ProDistill is training-based.

The most direct difference is the optimization procedure. ProDistill trains the merging coefficients 𝝀t(ℓ)\bm{\lambda}^{(\ell)}_{t} using gradient descent. Although the optimization is restricted to one layer at a time, it still requires iterative updates, gradients, learning-rate choices, optimizer states, and stopping criteria.

SLOA, in contrast, is training-free. For each local operator, SLOA solves a regularized least-squares problem in closed form:

(62) 𝜽merge=arg⁡min𝜽∈Θamb​ℒact​(𝜽)+1T​∑t=1T‖𝜽−𝜽t‖χ^t2.\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}=\underset{\bm{\theta}\in\Theta_{\mathrm{amb}}}{\arg\min}\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}(\bm{\theta})+\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\|_{\widehat{\chi}_{t}}^{2}.

The closed-form solution is possible because SLOA chooses local functional operators whose behavior maps are linear with respect to 𝜽\bm{\theta}. Thus, SLOA does not learn merging coefficients by gradient descent; it directly solves for the merged local operator.

SLOA merges local functional operators, whereas ProDistill merges task-vector parameter coordinates.

ProDistill retains the standard task-vector parameterization. For each layer, the merged layer remains in the affine span

(63) 𝜽0(ℓ)+span∘⁡{𝝉1(ℓ),…,𝝉T(ℓ)},\bm{\theta}_{0}^{(\ell)}+\operatorname{span}_{\circ}\left\{\bm{\tau}^{(\ell)}_{1},\ldots,\bm{\tau}^{(\ell)}_{T}\right\},

where the coefficients act element-wise on the task-vector coordinates. This gives ProDistill a flexible parameter-space interpolation mechanism, but the primitive objects being combined are still the original parameter tensors.

SLOA instead changes the unit of merging. In transformer attention, the individual matrices 𝑾Q,𝑾K,𝑾V,𝑾O{\bm{W}}_{Q},{\bm{W}}_{K},{\bm{W}}_{V},{\bm{W}}_{O} are not the local functional units. The attention scores depend on the composed QK operator

(64) 𝜽QK=1dk​𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤,\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{QK}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}{\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top},
