and the logits depends on the composed VO operator

(65) 𝜽VO=𝑾V​𝑾O.\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{VO}}={\bm{W}}_{V}{\bm{W}}_{O}.

SLOA merges these composed operators directly. This distinction is central: ProDistill optimizes a block-level representation-matching objective over task-vector coefficients, while SLOA constructs a local operator-level objective over the functional objects that determine the computation.

SLOA removes attention-factorization ambiguity by construction.

Attention heads have internal reparameterization symmetries. For any invertible matrix 𝑹{\bm{R}},

(66) 𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤=(𝑾Q​𝑹)​(𝑾K​𝑹−⁣⊤)⊤.{\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top}=({\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{R}})({\bm{W}}_{K}{\bm{R}}^{-\top})^{\top}.

Thus, two attention heads can produce identical QK score operators while using different query/key coordinates. An analogous ambiguity exists for the value/output factors. Any method that operates directly on the individual matrices 𝑾Q,𝑾K,𝑾V,𝑾O{\bm{W}}_{Q},{\bm{W}}_{K},{\bm{W}}_{V},{\bm{W}}_{O} must handle this coordinate ambiguity implicitly.

ProDistill uses an activation loss, so its objective can partially compensate for poor parameter-space interpolation. However, its parameterization still acts on the individual task-vector coordinates of the original projection matrices. It does not explicitly identify the invariant QK and VO operators, nor does it merge in the quotient space induced by attention-head reparameterizations. Consequently, the factorization ambiguity remains inside the optimization problem.

SLOA removes this ambiguity before solving the merge. Since the optimization variable is the composed operator itself, two different factorizations that realize the same QK or VO operator correspond to the same object in SLOA. The merged operator is therefore invariant to internal changes of head coordinates, and factorization is postponed until after the operator has been aligned.

SLOA is more fine-grained than layer-wise distillation inside transformer blocks.

ProDistill progresses layer by layer. The layer is treated as the unit whose output representation should match the teacher representation. This is a general design and can be applied to nonlinear modules because the optimization is performed by gradient descent.

SLOA instead uses a topological order over local operators inside the network. For a transformer block, SLOA can separately align LayerNorm affine maps, standard linear maps, QK attention operators, and VO attention operators. This allows the method to respect the internal computational structure of attention rather than treating the whole attention layer or block as a single black-box feature map. In particular, SLOA distinguishes the two roles of self-attention:

  • •

    the QK operator determines token-token routing through the pre-softmax attention scores;

  • •

    the VO operator determines what information is written back to the logit after attention weights are applied.

This decomposition is absent from ProDistill. ProDistill aligns block outputs, whereas SLOA aligns the local functional mechanisms that produce those outputs.

Both methods are progressive, but the progressive state has a different meaning.

Both ProDistill and SLOA use a progressive procedure in which later modules are merged under activations affected by earlier merges. However, the role of these activations differs.

In ProDistill, the progressive state consists of paired features (z1,z2)(z_{1},z_{2}), where z1z_{1} is produced by the partially merged student and z2z_{2} is produced by the corresponding teacher. The layer objective trains task-vector coefficients so that the student layer output matches the teacher layer output on these paired inputs.

In SLOA, the progressive state defines the local inputs 𝒁^t,i(m)\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{(m)} received by the partially merged model and 𝒁t,i(m){\bm{Z}}_{t,i}^{(m)} received by the task model. The merged operator is evaluated on the former, while the target output is generated by the task-specific local operator on the latter:

(67) 𝒜⁡(𝒁^t,i(m),𝜽)≈𝒜⁡(𝒁t,i(m),𝜽t(m)).\mathcal{A}\left(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{(m)};\bm{\theta}\right)\approx\mathcal{A}\left({\bm{Z}}_{t,i}^{(m)};\bm{\theta}^{(m)}_{t}\right).

Thus, SLOA is progressive at the level of local operator alignment, not at the level of learned task-vector coefficients. Each merge is corrective under the actual execution path of the partially merged network, while still solving a closed-form local regression problem.

SLOA decouples operator alignment from factorization rank.

A further distinction is architectural capacity. ProDistill keeps the original model architecture and learns coefficients for the existing task-vector parameters. In particular, an attention head retains the original head dimension. Thus, ProDistill does not create a mechanism for increasing the rank of the QK or VO operators after merging.

SLOA explicitly separates the ambient operator from its final factorization. For a head with original dimension dkd_{k}, each task-specific QK or VO operator has rank at most dkd_{k}. However, the merged multi-task operator may have larger effective rank because different tasks can use different singular directions. SLOA first solves for the merged operator in the ambient space Θamb=ℝd×d\Theta_{\mathrm{amb}}=\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} and only afterward factorizes it at a chosen rank rr. When r=dkr=d_{k}, SLOA preserves the original head width. When r>dkr>d_{k}, SLOA retains additional singular directions supported by the aligned operator. This rank-expansion mechanism is not available in ProDistill, because ProDistill does not decouple the merged attention operator from its original factorization.

The two methods make different trade-offs.

ProDistill is a general distillation-based merging framework. Its strength is that it can optimize feature matching for arbitrary modules without requiring the module to be linear in a chosen operator. This generality comes at the cost of gradient-based optimization and a parameter-coordinate task-vector representation.

SLOA makes the opposite trade-off. It focuses on modules that admit a local behavior map linear in an appropriate operator. This restriction enables closed-form merging, data-dependent operator geometry, attention-operator invariance, and post-merge rank control. Therefore, SLOA is not simply a training-free variant of ProDistill. It changes the mathematical object being merged: from task-vector coordinates trained to match layer features, to local functional operators solved by sequential regularized regression.

Appendix D Detailed derivation of local operator alignment

As described in §3, the Sequential Local Operator Alignment (SLOA) method merges a single operator at a time. By explicitly writing the term ℒact​(𝜽)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{act}}(\bm{\theta}), the unified loss objective for merging is defined as:

(68) L⁡(𝜽)=1T​∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt‖𝒜⁡(𝒁^t,i,𝜽)−𝒜⁡(𝒁t,i,𝜽t)‖F2+‖𝜽−𝜽t‖χ^t2)L(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\left\|\mathcal{A}(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta})-\mathcal{A}({\bm{Z}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta}_{t})\right\|_{F}^{2}+\left\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\|_{\widehat{\chi}_{t}}^{2}\right)
(69) 𝜽merge=arg⁡min𝜽∈Θamb​L​(𝜽)\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}=\underset{\bm{\theta}\in\Theta_{\mathrm{amb}}}{\arg\min}\;L(\bm{\theta})

Here, χ^t={𝒁^t,i}i=1nt\widehat{\chi}_{t}=\{\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\}_{i=1}^{n_{t}} is the collection of local inputs produced by the partially merged model. For standard linear operators and QK operator that taking only the activation as input, 𝒁^t,i=𝑿^t,i∈ℝL×d\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}=\widehat{{\bm{X}}}_{t,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}, while for components like the VO circuit, it also includes the composed attention matrix.

Now, for each operator, we will show how this unified loss objective can be reduced to a structured regression problem with a closed-form solution. We will also detail the explicit form of the data-dependent regularization term and the ambient operator space Θamb\Theta_{\mathrm{amb}} for each component, applying constraints (such as rank) during the subsequent factorization step for each operators mentioned in §3.1.

D.1 Optimal QK Operator

For the Query-Key circuit, for each attention head jj, let 𝑾Q(j),𝑾K(j)∈ℝd×dk{\bm{W}}_{Q}^{(j)},{\bm{W}}_{K}^{(j)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{k}} denote the query and key matrices, respectively. The consolidated score operator is defined as 𝜽(j)=1dk​𝑾Q(j)​𝑾K(j)⊤∈ℝd×d\bm{\theta}^{(j)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}{\bm{W}}_{Q}^{(j)}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{(j)\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. Since the operation acts bilinearly on the input representations, when evaluated on a single calibration example ii from task tt, the behavior map and the customized task-level regularization term are defined as:

(70) 𝒜⁡(𝒁^t,i,𝜽(𝒋))=𝒁^t,i​𝜽(𝒋)​𝒁^t,i⊤,‖𝜽(𝒋)−𝜽(𝒋)t‖χ^t2=‖𝚲t1/2​(𝜽(𝒋)−𝜽(𝒋)t)​𝚲t1/2‖F2\displaystyle\mathcal{A}(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta^{(j)}})=\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\bm{\theta^{(j)}}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top},\quad\left\|\bm{\theta^{(j)}}-\bm{\theta^{(j)}}_{t}\right\|_{\widehat{\chi}_{t}}^{2}=\left\|{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}^{1/2}(\bm{\theta^{(j)}}-\bm{\theta^{(j)}}_{t}){\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}^{1/2}\right\|_{F}^{2}

where 𝚲t∈ℝd×d{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is a diagonal precision matrix derived from the partially merged state collection χ^t\widehat{\chi}_{t}, and 𝚲t1/2{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}^{1/2} is its principal square root. Hereafter, we drop the head index jj for notational brevity, as the alignment is solved independently for each head.

To find the optimal operator, we first relax the rank-dkd_{k} structural constraint Θamb\Theta_{\mathrm{amb}} to solve for an unconstrained consolidated operator (the rank constraint is subsequently enforced via Singular Value Decomposition). Substituting the behavior map into the unified loss objective (68) and writing 𝒜⁡(𝒁t,i,𝜽t)=𝒀t,i\mathcal{A}({\bm{Z}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta}_{t})={\bm{Y}}_{t,i} as target, we have:

(71) L⁡(𝜽)=1T​∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt‖𝒁^t,i​𝜽​𝒁^t,i⊤−𝒀t,i‖F2+‖𝚲t1/2​(𝜽−𝜽t)​𝚲t1/2‖F2)L(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\left\|\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\bm{\theta}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}-{\bm{Y}}_{t,i}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\left\|{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}^{1/2}(\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t}){\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}^{1/2}\right\|_{F}^{2}\right)

where ntn_{t} is the number of calibration samples for task tt.

Because the relaxed objective function L⁡(𝜽)L(\bm{\theta}) is strictly convex, the global minimum is found by setting the gradient with respect to 𝜽\bm{\theta} to zero. Utilizing the matrix derivative identity ∇𝜽‖𝑨​𝜽​𝑨⊤−𝒀‖F2=2​𝑨⊤​(𝑨​𝜽​𝑨⊤−𝒀)​𝑨\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\|{\bm{A}}\bm{\theta}{\bm{A}}^{\top}-{\bm{Y}}\|_{F}^{2}=2{\bm{A}}^{\top}({\bm{A}}\bm{\theta}{\bm{A}}^{\top}-{\bm{Y}}){\bm{A}} and the linearity of the gradient over the finite sum, we obtain:

(72) ∇𝜽L​(𝜽)=2T​∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt𝒁^t,i⊤​(𝒁^t,i​𝜽​𝒁^t,i⊤−𝒀t,i)​𝒁^t,i+𝚲t​(𝜽−𝜽t)​𝚲t)=0\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}L(\bm{\theta})=\frac{2}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}\left(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\bm{\theta}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}-{\bm{Y}}_{t,i}\right)\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}+{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}(\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t}){\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\right)=0

Dividing by the scalar 2T\frac{2}{T} and distributing the terms inside the summations gives:

(73) ∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt(𝒁^t,i⊤​𝒁^t,i​𝜽​𝒁^t,i⊤​𝒁^t,i−𝒁^t,i⊤​𝒀t,i​𝒁^t,i)+𝚲t​𝜽​𝚲t−𝚲t​𝜽t​𝚲t)=0\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\left(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\bm{\theta}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}-\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}{\bm{Y}}_{t,i}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\right)+{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\bm{\theta}{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}-{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\bm{\theta}_{t}{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\right)=0

We group the terms dependent on the merged parameter 𝜽\bm{\theta} on the left-hand side, and move the constant target terms to the right-hand side:

(74) ∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt(𝒁^t,i⊤​𝒁^t,i​𝜽​𝒁^t,i⊤​𝒁^t,i)+𝚲t​𝜽​𝚲t)=∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt(𝒁^t,i⊤​𝒀t,i​𝒁^t,i)+𝚲t​𝜽t​𝚲t)\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\left(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\bm{\theta}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\right)+{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\bm{\theta}{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\right)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\left(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}{\bm{Y}}_{t,i}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\right)+{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\bm{\theta}_{t}{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\right)

To solve Equation 74 analytically, we define 𝑹t,i=𝒁^t,i⊤​𝒁^t,i∈ℝd×d{\bm{R}}_{t,i}=\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, and let 𝑪∈ℝd×d{\bm{C}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} denote the right-hand side constant matrix. The equation simplifies to:

(75) ∑t=1T([1nt​∑i=1nt𝑹t,i​𝜽​𝑹t,i]+𝚲t​𝜽​𝚲t)=𝑪\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\left[\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}{\bm{R}}_{t,i}\bm{\theta}{\bm{R}}_{t,i}\right]+{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\bm{\theta}{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\right)={\bm{C}}

To isolate 𝜽\bm{\theta}, we apply the vectorization operator vec⁡(⋅)\operatorname{vec}(\cdot). Using the Kronecker product identity vec⁡(𝑨​𝜽​𝑩)=(𝑩⊤⊗𝑨)​vec⁡(𝜽)\operatorname{vec}({\bm{A}}\bm{\theta}{\bm{B}})=({\bm{B}}^{\top}\otimes{\bm{A}})\operatorname{vec}(\bm{\theta}) and noting that both 𝑹t,i{\bm{R}}_{t,i} and 𝚲t{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t} are symmetric, we obtain:

(76) ∑t=1T([1nt​∑i=1nt(𝑹t,i⊗𝑹t,i)]+(𝚲t⊗𝚲t))​vec⁡(𝜽)=vec⁡(𝑪)\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\left[\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}({\bm{R}}_{t,i}\otimes{\bm{R}}_{t,i})\right]+({\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\otimes{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t})\right)\operatorname{vec}(\bm{\theta})=\operatorname{vec}({\bm{C}})

By defining the aggregated precision matrix 𝑯∈ℝd2×d2{\bm{H}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d^{2}\times d^{2}} as the operator on the left-hand side, the system reduces to the linear form:

(77) 𝑯​vec⁡(𝜽)=vec⁡(𝑪){\bm{H}}\operatorname{vec}(\bm{\theta})=\operatorname{vec}({\bm{C}})

Assuming 𝑯{\bm{H}} is invertible (or utilizing the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse 𝑯†{\bm{H}}^{\dagger} in rank-deficient scenarios), we isolate the vectorized parameters and apply the inverse vectorization operator to recover the optimal unconstrained operator 𝜽merge∈ℝd×d\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}:

(78) 𝜽merge=vec−1⁡(𝑯−1​vec⁡(𝑪))□\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}=\operatorname{vec}^{-1}\left({\bm{H}}^{-1}\operatorname{vec}({\bm{C}})\right)\quad\square

The above derivation yields an exact closed-form analytical solution for the optimal QK operator, which is subsequently factorized into 𝑾^Q\widehat{{\bm{W}}}_{Q} and 𝑾^K\widehat{{\bm{W}}}_{K} via SVD to reintroduce the rank constraint.

Computational Remark. While Equation 78 provides an exact analytical equality, directly materializing and inverting the Kronecker matrix 𝑯{\bm{H}} incurs an intractable time complexity of 𝒪⁡(d6)\mathcal{O}(d^{6}) and space complexity of 𝒪⁡(d4)\mathcal{O}(d^{4}). For standard Transformer dimensions (e.g., d≥768d\geq 768), this is computationally prohibitive. Therefore, in practice, we compute the optimal 𝜽merge\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}} iteratively without ever materializing 𝑯{\bm{H}} by employing the Conjugate Gradient (CG) algorithm 11 1 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_gradient_method.

D.1.1 Rank-Constrained Factorization of the QK Operator

Following the unconstrained optimization derived in §D.1, the optimal consolidated operator 𝜽merge∈ℝd×d\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} must be projected back onto the structural constraints of the attention mechanism. By the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem, the optimal rank-rr approximation in the Frobenius norm is obtained via the truncated Singular Value Decomposition (SVD):

(79) 𝜽merge=𝑼​𝚺​𝑽⊤⟹𝜽merge(r)=𝑼r​𝚺r​𝑽r⊤\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}={\bm{U}}{\bm{\Sigma}}{\bm{V}}^{\top}\quad\implies\quad\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}^{(r)}={\bm{U}}_{r}{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r}{\bm{V}}_{r}^{\top}

where 𝑼r,𝑽r∈ℝd×r{\bm{U}}_{r},{\bm{V}}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} contain the top rr left and right singular vectors, respectively, and 𝚺r∈ℝr×r{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r} is the diagonal matrix of the top rr singular values. The standard attention mechanism computes the QK logit matrix as 1c​𝑾^Q​𝑾^K⊤\frac{1}{c}\widehat{{\bm{W}}}_{Q}\widehat{{\bm{W}}}_{K}^{\top}, where cc is the attention scaling denominator (e.g., c=rc=\sqrt{r} or c=dkc=\sqrt{d_{k}}). To satisfy the equality 1c​𝑾^Q​𝑾^K⊤=𝜽merge(r)\frac{1}{c}\widehat{{\bm{W}}}_{Q}\widehat{{\bm{W}}}_{K}^{\top}=\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}^{(r)}, we distribute the singular values and the scalar cc symmetrically across the QK weight matrices:

(80) 𝑾^Q\displaystyle\widehat{{\bm{W}}}_{Q} =𝑼r​(c​𝚺r)1/2∈ℝd×r\displaystyle={\bm{U}}_{r}(c{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r})^{1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}
(81) 𝑾^K\displaystyle\widehat{{\bm{W}}}_{K} =𝑽r​(c​𝚺r)1/2∈ℝd×r\displaystyle={\bm{V}}_{r}(c{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r})^{1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}

D.2 Optimal VO Operator

For value-output (VO) circuits, for each head jj, we have 𝑾V(j)∈ℝd×dk{\bm{W}}_{V}^{(j)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{k}} as the value matrix, and 𝑾O(j)∈ℝdk×d{\bm{W}}_{O}^{(j)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times d} as the output matrix. The consolidated operator is defined as 𝜽(j)=𝑾V(j)​𝑾O(j)∈ℝd×d\bm{\theta}^{(j)}={\bm{W}}_{V}^{(j)}{\bm{W}}_{O}^{(j)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. In accordance with the sequential topological ordering described in §3, the VO operator takes as input the activation 𝑿^t,i\widehat{{\bm{X}}}_{t,i} as well as the attention matrix 𝑨^t,i∈ℝL×L\widehat{{\bm{A}}}_{t,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times L}, which is computed using the previously aligned QK operator. We explicitly define the partially merged local input state as 𝒁^t,i=𝑨^t,i​𝑿^t,i\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}=\widehat{{\bm{A}}}_{t,i}\widehat{{\bm{X}}}_{t,i}. The operation of the VO circuit is linear with respect to the input representations, and thus when evaluated on a single calibration example ii from task tt, the behavior map and the customized task-level regularization term are defined as:

(82) 𝒜⁡(𝒁^t,i,𝜽)=𝒁^t,i​𝜽,‖𝜽−𝜽t‖χ^t2=‖𝚲t1/2​(𝜽−𝜽t)‖F2\displaystyle\mathcal{A}(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta})=\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\bm{\theta},\quad\left\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\|_{\widehat{\chi}_{t}}^{2}=\left\|{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}^{1/2}(\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t})\right\|_{F}^{2}

where χ^t={𝒁^t,i}i=1nt\widehat{\chi}_{t}=\{\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\}_{i=1}^{n_{t}} representing attention-weighted input representations. Similar to the QK case, we droped jj for ease of notaion, since the same operation is opertated for each attention head. 𝚲t{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t} is a diagonal matrix derived from the attention score weighted partially merged state collection χ^t\widehat{\chi}_{t}, and 𝚲t1/2{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}^{1/2} is its square root.

For the VO operator, we solve for L⁡(𝜽)L(\bm{\theta}) with the structural constraint Θamb={rank(𝜽)≤r}\Theta_{\mathrm{amb}}=\{rank(\bm{\theta})\leq r\}. Substituting these into the unified objective function (5) and writing 𝒜⁡(𝒁t,i,𝜽t)=𝒀t,i\mathcal{A}({\bm{Z}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta}_{t})={\bm{Y}}_{t,i} as target yields:

(83) L⁡(𝜽)=1T​∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt‖𝒁^t,i​𝜽−𝒀t,i‖F2+‖𝚲t1/2​(𝜽−𝜽t)‖F2)L(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\left\|\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\bm{\theta}-{\bm{Y}}_{t,i}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\left\|{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}^{1/2}(\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t})\right\|_{F}^{2}\right)
(84) 𝜽merge=arg⁡min𝜽∈{rank(𝜽)≤r}​L​(𝜽)\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}=\underset{\bm{\theta}\in\{rank(\bm{\theta})\leq r\}}{\arg\min}\;L(\bm{\theta})

To solve this rank-constrained minimization problem, we first eliminate the summations by stacking the task-specific matrices vertically. Because scaling the objective by a constant TT does not alter the minimization, minimizing L⁡(𝜽)L(\bm{\theta}) is strictly equivalent to minimizing a single, consolidated Frobenius norm:

(85) minrank⁡(𝜽)≤r⁡‖𝒁^​𝜽−𝒀^‖F2\min_{\operatorname{rank}(\bm{\theta})\leq r}\left\|\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}\bm{\theta}-\widehat{{\bm{Y}}}\right\|_{F}^{2}

where augmented matrices 𝒁^\widehat{{\bm{Z}}} and 𝒀^\widehat{{\bm{Y}}} are defined as:

𝒁^=[𝒁^1,1𝒁^1,n1𝒁^T,1𝒁^T,nT𝚲11/2𝚲T1/2]𝒀^=[𝒀1,1𝒀1,n1𝒀T,1𝒀T,nT𝚲11/2​𝜽1𝚲T1/2​𝜽T]\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}=\begin{bmatrix}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{1,1}\\ \vdots\\ \widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{1,n_{1}}\\ \vdots\\ \widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{T,1}\\ \vdots\\ \widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{T,n_{T}}\\ {\bm{\Lambda}}_{1}^{1/2}\\ \vdots\\ {\bm{\Lambda}}_{T}^{1/2}\end{bmatrix}\quad\widehat{{\bm{Y}}}=\begin{bmatrix}{\bm{Y}}_{1,1}\\ \vdots\\ {\bm{Y}}_{1,n_{1}}\\ \vdots\\ {\bm{Y}}_{T,1}\\ \vdots\\ {\bm{Y}}_{T,n_{T}}\\ {\bm{\Lambda}}_{1}^{1/2}\bm{\theta}_{1}\\ \vdots\\ {\bm{\Lambda}}_{T}^{1/2}\bm{\theta}_{T}\end{bmatrix}

Let truncr⁡(⋅)\operatorname{trunc}_{r}(\cdot) denote the truncated Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) operator that retains only the top rr singular components of a matrix. The exact closed-form solution for this rank-constrained objective is given by Friedland and Torokhti [2007]:

(86) 𝜽merge=(𝒁^⊤𝒁^)−1/2truncr[(𝒁^⊤𝒁^)−1/2𝒁^⊤𝒀^]\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}=(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}^{\top}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}})^{-1/2}\operatorname{trunc}_{r}\!\left[(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}^{\top}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}})^{-1/2}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}^{\top}\widehat{{\bm{Y}}}\right]

Crucially, we do not need to explicitly materialize the massive stacked matrices 𝒁^\widehat{{\bm{Z}}} and 𝒀^\widehat{{\bm{Y}}}. By computing the inner products of the block matrices, they elegantly collapse back into the 𝑮^t\widehat{\bm{G}}_{t} and 𝑪^t\widehat{\bm{C}}_{t} matrices:

(87) 𝑮^t\displaystyle\widehat{{\bm{G}}}_{t} =∑i=1nt1nt​𝒁^t,i⊤​𝒁^t,i+𝚲t\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\frac{1}{n_{t}}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}+{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}
(88) 𝑪^t\displaystyle\widehat{{\bm{C}}}_{t} =∑i=1nt1nt​𝒁^t,i⊤​𝒀t,i+𝚲t​𝜽t\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\frac{1}{n_{t}}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}{\bm{Y}}_{t,i}+{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\bm{\theta}_{t}

Substituting these sums back into the solution, we obtain the final closed-form equation for the rank-constrained VO operator:

(89) 𝜽merge=(∑t=1T𝑮^t)−1/2truncr[(∑t=1T𝑮^t)−1/2(∑t=1T𝑪^t)]□\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}=\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\widehat{{\bm{G}}}_{t}\right)^{-1/2}\operatorname{trunc}_{r}\!\left[\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\widehat{{\bm{G}}}_{t}\right)^{-1/2}\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\widehat{{\bm{C}}}_{t}\right)\right]\square

D.2.1 Factorization of the VO operator

After solving our rank constraint solution for VO operator, we need to factorize the optimal merged parameter back to 𝑾^V\widehat{{\bm{W}}}_{V} and 𝑾^O\widehat{{\bm{W}}}_{O}.

(90) 𝜽merge=𝑼​𝚺​𝑽⊤⟹𝜽merge(r)=𝑼r​𝚺r​𝑽r⊤\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}={\bm{U}}{\bm{\Sigma}}{\bm{V}}^{\top}\quad\implies\quad\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{merge}}^{(r)}={\bm{U}}_{r}{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r}{\bm{V}}_{r}^{\top}

where 𝑼r,𝑽r∈ℝd×r{\bm{U}}_{r},{\bm{V}}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} contain the top rr left and right singular vectors, respectively, and 𝚺r∈ℝr×r{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r} is the diagonal matrix of the top rr singular values. Unlike QK circuit, there is no scaling factor in OV circuit of standard attention Therefore the factorization follows:

(91) 𝑾^V\displaystyle\widehat{{\bm{W}}}_{V} =𝑼r​𝚺r1/2∈ℝd×r\displaystyle={\bm{U}}_{r}{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r}^{1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}
(92) 𝑾^O\displaystyle\widehat{{\bm{W}}}_{O} =𝑽r​𝚺r1/2∈ℝd×r\displaystyle={\bm{V}}_{r}{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r}^{1/2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}

D.3 Optimal MLP operator

For MLP layers, the behavior map is defined as and the regularization term is defined as:

(93) 𝒜⁡(𝒁^t,i,𝜽)=𝒁^t,i​𝜽,‖𝜽−𝜽t‖χ^t2=‖𝚲t1/2​(𝜽−𝜽t)‖F2\mathcal{A}(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta})=\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\bm{\theta},\quad\left\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\|_{\widehat{\chi}_{t}}^{2}=\left\|{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}^{1/2}(\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t})\right\|_{F}^{2}

Unlike the VO circuit, the MLP layer does not have a low-rank bottleneck constraint. Therefore, we can directly solve for the optimal operator 𝜽\bm{\theta} without imposing any structural constraints. Substituting these into the unified objective function Eq. (68) and and writing 𝒜⁡(𝒁t,i,𝜽t)=𝒀t,i\mathcal{A}({\bm{Z}}_{t,i};\bm{\theta}_{t})={\bm{Y}}_{t,i} as target yields:

(94) L⁡(𝜽)=1T​∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt‖𝒁^t,i​𝜽−𝒀t,i‖F2+‖𝚲t1/2​(𝜽−𝜽t)‖F2)L(\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\left\|\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\bm{\theta}-{\bm{Y}}_{t,i}\right\|_{F}^{2}+\left\|{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}^{1/2}(\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t})\right\|_{F}^{2}\right)

The objective reeduced to standard regularized multivariate least squares problem (i.e., ridge regression under a Mahalanobis prior), and the closed-form solution can be derived by setting the gradient to zero. The optimal operator 𝜽\bm{\theta} is given by:

(95) ∇𝜽L​(𝜽)=2T​∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt𝒁^t,i⊤​(𝒁^t,i​𝜽−𝒀t,i)+𝚲t​(𝜽−𝜽t))=0\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}L({\bm{\theta}})=\frac{2}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}(\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}\bm{\theta}-{\bm{Y}}_{t,i})+{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}(\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t})\right)=0

Rearranging the terms, we obtain:

(96) (∑t=1T1nt​∑i=1nt𝒁^t,i⊤​𝒁^t,i+𝚲t)​𝜽=∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt𝒁^t,i⊤​𝒀t,i+𝚲t​𝜽t)\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}+{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\right)\bm{\theta}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}{\bm{Y}}_{t,i}+{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\bm{\theta}_{t}\right)

Let us define Gram matrix 𝑮^t\widehat{{\bm{G}}}_{t} and cross-covariance matrix 𝑪^t\widehat{{\bm{C}}}_{t} as:

(97) 𝑮^t=1nt​∑i=1nt𝒁^t,i⊤​𝒁^t,i+𝚲t,𝑪^t=1nt​∑i=1nt𝒁^t,i⊤​𝒀t,i+𝚲t​𝜽t\widehat{{\bm{G}}}_{t}=\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}+{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t},\quad\widehat{{\bm{C}}}_{t}=\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\widehat{{\bm{Z}}}_{t,i}^{\top}{\bm{Y}}_{t,i}+{\bm{\Lambda}}_{t}\bm{\theta}_{t}

The closed-form solution for the optimal MLP operator is then given by:

(98) 𝜽=(∑t=1T𝑮^t)−1​(∑t=1T𝑪^t)​□\bm{\theta}=\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\widehat{{\bm{G}}}_{t}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\widehat{{\bm{C}}}_{t}\right)\square

D.4 Optimal LayerNorm Operator

For the Layer Normalization module, the operator consists of a scale vector 𝜸∈ℝd\bm{\gamma}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and a bias vector 𝜷∈ℝd\bm{\beta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Evaluated on a single calibration example ii from task tt, the behavior map and the data-dependent regularization term are defined as:

(99) 𝒜⁡(𝑿^t,i,𝜸,𝜷)\displaystyle\mathcal{A}(\widehat{{\bm{X}}}_{t,i};\bm{\gamma},\bm{\beta}) =ν⁡(𝑿^t,i)​diag⁡(𝜸)+𝟏​𝜷⊤\displaystyle=\nu(\widehat{{\bm{X}}}_{t,i})\operatorname{diag}(\bm{\gamma})+\mathbf{1}\bm{\beta}^{\top}
(100) ‖𝜽−𝜽t‖χ^t2\displaystyle\left\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\theta}_{t}\right\|_{\widehat{\chi}_{t}}^{2} =‖𝚲γ,t1/2​(𝜸−𝜸t)‖22+‖𝚲β,t1/2​(𝜷−𝜷t)‖22\displaystyle=\left\|{\bm{\Lambda}}_{\gamma,t}^{1/2}(\bm{\gamma}-\bm{\gamma}_{t})\right\|_{2}^{2}+\left\|{\bm{\Lambda}}_{\beta,t}^{1/2}(\bm{\beta}-\bm{\beta}_{t})\right\|_{2}^{2}

where ν⁡(⋅)\nu(\cdot) denotes the normalization that zeroes the mean and scales to unit variance across the feature dimension, and 𝟏∈ℝL\mathbf{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{L} is a vector of ones. The diagonal precision matrices 𝚲γ,t{\bm{\Lambda}}_{\gamma,t} and 𝚲β,t{\bm{\Lambda}}_{\beta,t} govern the task-dependent geometry for the scale and bias, respectively.

Because the affine transformation acts independently on each feature dimension j∈{1,…,d}j\in\{1,\dots,d\}, the Frobenius norm cleanly decouples. We can therefore break the global objective into dd independent optimization problems.

Let 𝒙^t,i∈ℝL\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{t,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{L} denote the jj-th column of the normalized input ν⁡(𝑿^t,i)\nu(\widehat{{\bm{X}}}_{t,i}), and let 𝒚t,i∈ℝL{\bm{y}}_{t,i}\in\mathbb{R}^{L} denote the jj-th column of the target output 𝒀t,i{\bm{Y}}_{t,i}. Correspondingly, let the scalars γ,β∈ℝ\gamma,\beta\in\mathbb{R} denote the jj-th elements of the vectors 𝜸\bm{\gamma} and 𝜷\bm{\beta}, and let γt,βt∈ℝ\gamma_{t},\beta_{t}\in\mathbb{R} denote the jj-th elements of the task-specific parameters 𝜸t\bm{\gamma}_{t} and 𝜷t\bm{\beta}_{t}. Furthermore, let the scalars λγ,t,λβ,t∈ℝ\lambda_{\gamma,t},\lambda_{\beta,t}\in\mathbb{R} represent the jj-th diagonal entries of the precision matrices 𝚲γ,t{\bm{\Lambda}}_{\gamma,t} and 𝚲β,t{\bm{\Lambda}}_{\beta,t}. Dropping the feature dimension index jj for notational brevity, the objective for a single feature dimension over the empirical calibration mixture is:

(101) L⁡(γ,β)=1T​∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt‖𝒙^t,i​γ+𝟏​β−𝒚t,i‖22+λγ,t​(γ−γt)2+λβ,t​(β−βt)2)L(\gamma,\beta)=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\left\|\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{t,i}\gamma+\mathbf{1}\beta-{\bm{y}}_{t,i}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda_{\gamma,t}(\gamma-\gamma_{t})^{2}+\lambda_{\beta,t}(\beta-\beta_{t})^{2}\right)

Because this dimension-wise objective is strictly convex, we find the global minimum by setting the partial derivatives with respect to γ\gamma and β\beta to zero.

For the scale parameter γ\gamma, we obtain:

(102) ∂L∂γ=0⟹2T​∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt𝒙^t,i⊤​(𝒙^t,i​γ+𝟏​β−𝒚t,i)+λγ,t​(γ−γt))=0\displaystyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial\gamma}=0\implies\frac{2}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{t,i}^{\top}(\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{t,i}\gamma+\mathbf{1}\beta-{\bm{y}}_{t,i})+\lambda_{\gamma,t}(\gamma-\gamma_{t})\right)=0

Rearranging terms, we get:

(103) ∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt𝒙^t,i⊤​𝒙^t,i+λγ,t)​γ+∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt𝒙^t,i⊤​𝟏)​β=∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt𝒙^t,i⊤​𝒚t,i+λγ,t​γt)\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{t,i}^{\top}\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{t,i}+\lambda_{\gamma,t}\right)\gamma+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{t,i}^{\top}\mathbf{1}\right)\beta=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{t,i}^{\top}{\bm{y}}_{t,i}+\lambda_{\gamma,t}\gamma_{t}\right)

For the bias parameter β\beta, noting that 𝟏⊤​𝟏=L\mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{1}=L (the sequence length), we obtain:

∂L∂β=0\displaystyle\frac{\partial L}{\partial\beta}=0 ⟹2T​∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt𝟏⊤​(𝒙^t,i​γ+𝟏​β−𝒚t,i)+λβ,t​(β−βt))=0\displaystyle\implies\frac{2}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\mathbf{1}^{\top}(\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{t,i}\gamma+\mathbf{1}\beta-{\bm{y}}_{t,i})+\lambda_{\beta,t}(\beta-\beta_{t})\right)=0
(104) ⟹∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt𝟏⊤​𝒙^t,i)​γ+∑t=1T(L+λβ,t)​β=∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt𝟏⊤​𝒚t,i+λβ,t​βt)\displaystyle\implies\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{t,i}\right)\gamma+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(L+\lambda_{\beta,t}\right)\beta=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\mathbf{1}^{\top}{\bm{y}}_{t,i}+\lambda_{\beta,t}\beta_{t}\right)

Eq. (103) and (104) form a coupled system of two linear equations. To express the closed-form solution elegantly, we define the following scalar accumulators:

Sx​x\displaystyle S_{xx} =∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt𝒙^t,i⊤​𝒙^t,i+λγ,t),\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{t,i}^{\top}\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{t,i}+\lambda_{\gamma,t}\right),\quad Sx​y\displaystyle S_{xy} =∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt𝒙^t,i⊤​𝒚t,i+λγ,t​γt)\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{t,i}^{\top}{\bm{y}}_{t,i}+\lambda_{\gamma,t}\gamma_{t}\right)
S1\displaystyle S_{1} =∑t=1T(L+λβ,t),\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(L+\lambda_{\beta,t}\right),\quad Sy\displaystyle S_{y} =∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt𝟏⊤​𝒚t,i+λβ,t​βt)\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\mathbf{1}^{\top}{\bm{y}}_{t,i}+\lambda_{\beta,t}\beta_{t}\right)
Sx\displaystyle S_{x} =∑t=1T(1nt​∑i=1nt𝟏⊤​𝒙^t,i)\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{n_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\hat{{\bm{x}}}_{t,i}\right)

This coupled system cleanly reduces to a symmetric 2×22\times 2 matrix equation:

(105) [Sx​xSxSxS1]​[γβ]=[Sx​ySy]\begin{bmatrix}S_{xx}&S_{x}\\ S_{x}&S_{1}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\gamma\\ \beta\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}S_{xy}\\ S_{y}\end{bmatrix}

By inverting this 2×22\times 2 matrix (e.g., via Cramer’s rule), we obtain the exact closed-form solution for the optimal merged scale and bias parameters for this feature dimension:

(106) γ=S1​Sx​y−Sx​SySx​x​S1−Sx2β=Sx​x​Sy−Sx​Sx​ySx​x​S1−Sx2\gamma=\frac{S_{1}S_{xy}-S_{x}S_{y}}{S_{xx}S_{1}-S_{x}^{2}}\quad\beta=\frac{S_{xx}S_{y}-S_{x}S_{xy}}{S_{xx}S_{1}-S_{x}^{2}}

We can perform the same operation for each dimension of vectors, 𝜸\bm{\gamma} and 𝜷\bm{\beta}, in parallel to obtain the final solution.

D.5 Rank-controlled factorization of merged attention operators

This section details the factorization step summarized in §3.5.

Low-rank structure of attention heads.

Let dd be the residual-stream dimension and dkd_{k} the head dimension. For a single head, 𝑾Q,𝑾K,𝑾V∈ℝd×dk{\bm{W}}_{Q},{\bm{W}}_{K},{\bm{W}}_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{k}} and 𝑾O∈ℝdk×d{\bm{W}}_{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times d}, so the local operators

(107) 𝜽Q​K=𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤/dk,𝜽V​O=𝑾V​𝑾O\bm{\theta}_{QK}={\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{k}},\qquad\bm{\theta}_{VO}={\bm{W}}_{V}{\bm{W}}_{O}

are d×dd\times d matrices of rank at most dkd_{k}: each head implements a d×dd\times d operator through a width-dkd_{k} bottleneck. SLOA merges these operators in the ambient space Θamb=ℝd×d\Theta_{\mathrm{amb}}=\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, where no rank constraint is imposed, and restores a factorized form only afterwards. All steps below are applied independently to every head, and separately to its QK and VO operators.

Truncated SVD.

Given a merged operator 𝜽¯∈Θamb\bar{\bm{\theta}}\in\Theta_{\mathrm{amb}} with SVD 𝜽¯=𝑼​𝚺​𝑽⊤\bar{\bm{\theta}}={\bm{U}}{\bm{\Sigma}}{\bm{V}}^{\top}, let 𝑼r{\bm{U}}_{r}, 𝚺r{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r}, and 𝑽r{\bm{V}}_{r} retain the top rr singular directions. By the Eckart–Young theorem, 𝜽¯r=𝑼r​𝚺r​𝑽r⊤\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{r}={\bm{U}}_{r}{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r}{\bm{V}}_{r}^{\top} is the best rank-rr approximation of 𝜽¯\bar{\bm{\theta}} in Frobenius norm.

QK factorization.

Let τ\tau denote the attention scaling used after factorization: τ=dk\tau=\sqrt{d_{k}} if the default implementation is kept, or τ=r\tau=\sqrt{r} if the expanded head uses the standard scaling for width rr. Setting

(108) 𝑾Q=𝑼r​(τ​𝚺r)1/2,𝑾K=𝑽r​(τ​𝚺r)1/2{\bm{W}}_{Q}={\bm{U}}_{r}(\tau{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r})^{1/2},\qquad{\bm{W}}_{K}={\bm{V}}_{r}(\tau{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r})^{1/2}

gives 𝑾Q​𝑾K⊤/τ=𝜽¯Q​K,r{\bm{W}}_{Q}{\bm{W}}_{K}^{\top}/\tau=\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{QK,r} for either choice of τ\tau.

VO factorization.

The VO behavior map 𝑨​𝑿​𝜽V​O{\bm{A}}{\bm{X}}\bm{\theta}_{VO} has no scaling, so we set

(109) 𝑾V=𝑼r​𝚺r1/2,𝑾O=𝚺r1/2​𝑽r⊤,{\bm{W}}_{V}={\bm{U}}_{r}{\bm{\Sigma}}_{r}^{1/2},\qquad{\bm{W}}_{O}={\bm{\Sigma}}_{r}^{1/2}{\bm{V}}_{r}^{\top},

which gives 𝑾V​𝑾O=𝜽¯V​O,r{\bm{W}}_{V}{\bm{W}}_{O}=\bar{\bm{\theta}}_{VO,r}. In both cases the head width becomes rr while dd is unchanged. The QK and VO ranks may differ (rqkr_{\rm qk}, rovr_{\rm ov}; Fig. 7); unless stated otherwise, r=rqk=rovr=r_{\rm qk}=r_{\rm ov}.

Why the merged operator may need rank above dkd_{k}.

The rank rr controls how much of the merged operator’s spectrum is retained; r=dkr=d_{k} preserves the original head width. Different task models, however, may use different low-dimensional subspaces, and a combination of low-rank operators need not share their rank: the sum of two rank-one operators with different singular directions has rank two, and in general rank⁡(∑t𝜽t)\operatorname{rank}\bigl(\sum_{t}\bm{\theta}_{t}\bigr) can reach min⁡(d,T​dk)\min(d,\,Td_{k}). Truncating the merged operator back to dkd_{k} can therefore discard directions that are useful for multi-task behavior; r>dkr>d_{k} retains them.

Does rank expansion overfit?

Increasing rr beyond dkd_{k} adds capacity without gradient-based training, which might be expected to overfit the calibration set. It does not, however, introduce free parameters: the factorization only retains singular directions already present in the aligned operator 𝜽¯\bar{\bm{\theta}}, which is anchored to the task-specific operators by the regularizer in Eq. (5). Consistent with this, rank expansion did not reduce average accuracy in any of our settings and typically improved it (§4, §F.3). The cost is a wider head at inference, quantified in §G.3.

Appendix E Experimental details

E.1 Handiling bias terms

Many prior works treat weight matrices and bias terms differently during the merging operation, opting to simply average the bias terms across models. In contrast, we handle bias terms correctly with respect to our objective via an augmentation trick that applies uniformly to all linear layers, including MLPs and attention projections. For instance with weight matrix 𝑾∈ℝd×dout{\bm{W}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{\text{out}}} and bias 𝒃∈ℝdout{\bm{b}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}}, the standard forward pass for a batch of LL sequence length is:

(110) 𝒀=𝑿​𝑾+1L​𝒃⊤,𝑿∈ℝl×d,𝒀∈ℝL×dout.{\bm{Y}}={\bm{X}}{\bm{W}}+\textbf{1}_{L}{\bm{b}}^{\top},\qquad{\bm{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{l\times d},\quad{\bm{Y}}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d_{\text{out}}}.

We rewrite this compactly by augmenting the input and weight matrix:

(111) 𝒀=𝑿~​𝑾~,𝑿~=[𝑿∣1n]∈ℝl×(d+1),𝑾~=[𝑾𝒃⊤]∈ℝ(d+1)×dout.{\bm{Y}}=\tilde{{\bm{X}}}\,\tilde{{\bm{W}}},\qquad\tilde{{\bm{X}}}=\bigl[{\bm{X}}\mid\textbf{1}_{n}\bigr]\in\mathbb{R}^{l\times(d+1)},\qquad\tilde{{\bm{W}}}=\begin{bmatrix}{\bm{W}}\\ {\bm{b}}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(d+1)\times d_{\text{out}}}.

Our merging procedure operates directly on the augmented matrices {𝑾~t}t=1T\{\tilde{{\bm{W}}}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}, yielding 𝑾~merge∈ℝ(d+1)×dout\tilde{{\bm{W}}}_{\text{merge}}\in\mathbb{R}^{(d+1)\times d_{\text{out}}}. The merged weight matrix and bias are then recovered by partitioning. The same augmentation applies to the QK and VO operators, where the bias terms are absorbed into the augmented weight matrices.

E.2 Dataset description

E.2.1 Dataset for vision task.

In our vision model merging experiments, we utilize the datasets and task-specific fine-tuned checkpoints provided by the FusionBench framework [Tang et al., 2024]. We employ the Vision Transformer (ViT) variant of CLIP [Radford et al., 2021b] as our base architecture. Rather than appending a randomly initialized linear classification head during fine-tuning, these models retain CLIP’s native dual-encoder structure. Specifically, classification is formulated as a multi-modal contrastive task: the model computes the cosine similarity between the visual embedding of the input image and the textual embeddings generated by passing class-specific text prompts (e.g., “a photo of a {class}”) through the frozen text encoder. To maintain strict consistency with this paradigm, our evaluation reports the standard zero-shot classification accuracy utilizing these text-driven prototypes. The datasets used for model merging are listed in Table 5. We also report the calibration set size and the percentage of the training set used for calibration. The calibration set size is fixed at 256 samples across all datasets, which represents a small fraction of the training data.

E.2.2 Dataset for NLU task.

For language model experiments, we use model checkpoints from the DARE [Yu et al., 2024] work. We evaluate the performance of these models on the 7 GLUE benchmark [Wang et al., 2019],22 2 https://huggingface.co/datasets/nyu-mll/glue , which covers a range of NLU tasks, including grammatical acceptability (CoLA), natural language classification (MNLI, RTE, QNLI), semantic equivalence (MRPC, QQP), and sentiment analysis (SST-2). The dataset statistics and evaluation metrics for these tasks are summarized in Table 6. We use standard training and validation splits for each task, and we set aside a small calibration set of 256 examples from the training set to perform model merging. The percentage of the calibration set relative to the training set is also reported in the table.

E.2.3 Dataset for LLM experiments

For the LLM merging experiments, we did not use an off-the-shelf pool of LoRA experts for LLaMA-2-7B [Touvron et al., 2023]; instead, we constructed our own task pool. We train three LoRA experts [Hu et al., 2022] independently from the LLaMA-2-7B base checkpoint, each targeting all linear projections at rank 32(α=64\alpha{=}64), for 3 epochs with a cosine learning-rate schedule (peak learning rate 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}) and an effective batch size of 32: a math expert on MetaMathQA [Yu et al., 2023], a code expert on Magicoder-Evol-Instruct-110K [Wei et al., 2024], and an instruction-following expert on the persona-conditioned instruction-following split of Tulu-3-SFT [Lambert et al., 2025]. Each expert is trained with a single, fixed prompt template applied to every example (the code expert uses Magicoder’s own instruction/response wrapper; the math and instruction-following experts share an Alpaca-style instruction/response template) see 4, and the same template is reused uniformly at both calibration and evaluation time. We evaluate each task on its corresponding standard benchmark rather than a held-out split of its own training corpus: GSM8K [Cobbe et al., 2021] for math (exact-match accuracy under flexible answer extraction), HumanEval [Chen et al., 2021] for code (pass@1), and IFEval [Zhou et al., 2023] for instruction-following (prompt-level strict accuracy).

All three are evaluated zero-shot through lm-evaluation-harness 33 3 https://github.com/eleutherai/lm-evaluation-harness, with each task’s training template baked into its eval prompt. Dataset statistics, calibration-set sizes, and calibration coverage (a fixed 256 examples per task, drawn from the same training split and formatted with the same template used for fine-tuning) are summarized in Table 7.

Appendix F Additional experiments and ablation analysis of SLOA

We study how SLOA scales with calibration data, rank expansion, and attention-circuit capacity. We also investigate the behavior of SLOA on LoRA finetuned models.

F.1 Scaling to a larger vision backbone: ViT-B/16

To test whether SLOA’s advantage persists as model capacity grows, we repeat the ViT-B/32 multi-task merging experiments (§4.1) on the larger ViT-B/16 backbone across the same 8-, 14-, and 20-task benchmarks (Table 8); as a complementary scaling direction, we also evaluate SLOA on a much larger, 7B-parameter decoder-only LLM in the main text (§4.3, Table 4). The trend mirrors ViT-B/32: SLOA’s margin over the best baseline widens as the number of merged tasks grows. On 8 tasks, the data-free baseline Iso-CTS is narrowly the strongest method overall (89.01 vs. 88.04 for SLOA (r=128r=128)); by 14 tasks, SLOA (85.16) has overtaken it (84.54); and by 20 tasks, SLOA leads by nearly 5 points (83.43 vs. 78.50). As on ViT-B/32, increasing rr from 64 to 128 improves performance at every task count, with the gain growing alongside the number of merged tasks. Ortiz-Jimenez et al. [2023] show that larger, better-pretrained vision backbones tend to be more weight-disentangled than smaller ones, so task-specific fine-tuning directions interfere less under simple weight-space combination. This may explain why data-free baselines remain competitive with SLOA on ViT-B/16 when only a few tasks are merged. However, as the number of merged tasks grows and interference increases, SLOA, which aligns functional operators rather than raw weights, wins by an increasingly clear margin.

F.2 Merging LoRA-adapted ViT experts

SLOA extends naturally to LoRA-adapted experts: there is no additional difficulty caused by the LoRA parameterization itself. For a LoRA-adapted task tt-weight Wt=W0+Δ​WtW_{t}=W_{0}+\Delta W_{t}, with Δ​Wt=Bt​At\Delta W_{t}=B_{t}A_{t}, we first form the effective fine-tuned weight WtW_{t} and then construct the same functional QK, VO, linear, and normalization operators used for fully fine-tuned experts; no change to the SLOA local objective is required. This distinction is important because LoRA’s factors are themselves non-identifiable: Bt​At=(Bt​R)​(R−1​At)B_{t}A_{t}=(B_{t}R)(R^{-1}A_{t}) for any invertible RR, so methods that operate separately on AtA_{t} and BtB_{t} can depend on an arbitrary low-rank coordinate system. SLOA does not merge the individual LoRA factors; it merges the effective functional operator and is therefore invariant to this factorization ambiguity. We evaluate this on ViT-B/32 LoRA experts (KnOTS checkpoints) [Stoica et al., 2025] across the same 8-task vision benchmark. Table 9 shows that SLOA achieves the highest normalized accuracy among all methods: SLOA (r=128r=128) reaches 88.07%, 7.0 points above the strongest baseline. Notably, even SLOA (r=64r=64) already exceeds all baselines at 82.66%, despite each task-specific LoRA update being rank 16 – reinforcing the view that the subspace spanned by the merged operator can exceed the rank of any individual task expert.

F.3 Scaling with calibration samples and rank

Figure 5 reports average accuracy as a function of calibration samples for vision (ViT-B/32 and ViT-B/16, 20 tasks) and language (RoBERTa, 7 tasks). Across both modalities and all rank configurations, SLOA improves steadily as calibration data increase. This is consistent with our unified objective in Eq. (5): larger calibration sets provide a better-conditioned system for estimating the merged weights. Notably, even with only 128 samples, our SLOA outperforms all baselines (see Tables 2 -16), demonstrating strong data efficiency. Increasing the rank from the default r=rqk=rov=64r=r_{\rm qk}=r_{\rm ov}=64 to 128128 and 256256 further improves performance. On vision tasks, higher rank consistently helps across sample sizes, reflecting the greater diversity of the 20-task setting. On NLU tasks, the improvement from 6464 to 128128 is clear, while 256256 gives diminishing returns, suggesting that the effective rank required for merging grows with task number and diversity.

F.4 Error accumulation across network depth

To directly assess whether and how merging error compounds across the network’s topological ordering of operators, we measure, at each vision-encoder block, the mean relative L2L_{2} error between the merged model’s activation and the corresponding task-specific expert’s activation, averaged across all 20 tasks. We report this on ViT-B/16 in the 20-task setting, the most challenging regime in our vision benchmarks, comparing SLOA (r∈{64,128,256}r\in\{64,128,256\}) against RegMean, RegMean++, and Iso-CTS (best performing data-free method). Figure 6(a) shows that error compounds with depth for every method, but at sharply different rates. Through the first six blocks, SLOA and RegMean++ track closely; the two only begin to diverge from block 7 onward, once upstream discrepancies have had several blocks to accumulate. SLOA’s error also grows more slowly relative to its own input-level error, peaking at 1.65–1.69×\times its starting value versus 1.87×\times for RegMean++ and 2.08×\times for RegMean. This depth-dependent divergence, rather than a uniform improvement at every block, localizes SLOA’s advantage to the later stages of the network, where uncorrected merging error would otherwise compound through the topological ordering of blocks. Expanding the rank from r=64r=64 to r=256r=256 narrows the error gap further.

F.5 Decoupling the QK and OV circuits

To test whether the QK and OV circuits should always use the same rank, we vary rqkr_{\rm qk} and rovr_{\rm ov} independently on ViT-B/32 with 20 tasks and 1024 calibration samples, while fixing the other rank at 64. Figure 7 shows three main trends. First, expanding either circuit alone improves performance only modestly and saturates after roughly r=256r=256. Second, QK expansion is more effective than OV expansion, indicating that query-key interactions are a stronger bottleneck for task-specific representation. Third, jointly expanding both circuits gives the best and most sustained gains. Thus, we conclude that the two circuits contribute complementary information, and therefore in practice, scaling rqkr_{\rm qk} and rovr_{\rm ov} together is the most effective design.

F.6 Sensitivity to regularization strength

The regularization term in Eq. (5) is controlled by α\alpha and stabilizes the solution when calibration data is limited. Figure 9 evaluates this effect on ViT-B/32 with 8 tasks. With few samples, especially 64 or 128, larger α\alpha improves performance by anchoring the solution toward the task-specific weights. With more samples, 256 or 512, the activation-alignment term is already sufficiently constrained, so strong regularization becomes unnecessary and can reduce performance. The optimal α\alpha therefore decreases as the calibration set grows, approaching α≈0.05\alpha\approx 0.05 at larger sample sizes. These results suggest that SLOA is robust to α\alpha when enough data is available, while the regularizer is most useful in the low-data regime.

F.7 Component ablation.

SLOA extends standard linear-layer merging with three components: sequential operator alignment, the QK operator, and the OV operator (§3.1). Figure 8 compares four configurations on ViT-B/32 with 20 tasks: sequential alignment with isolated weight merging, sequential alignment plus QK only, sequential alignment plus OV only, and the full SLOA. Sequential alignment alone is already strong, confirming that the sequential operator structure is a major source of improvement. However, adding only QK or only OV degrades performance, as the two circuits are tightly coupled inside self-attention; modifying one without the other introduces a functional error that propagates through later layers. In contrast, combining both operators recovers this loss and improves over sequential alignment alone, showing that QK and OV should be merged jointly.

F.8 Sequential correction versus training-free baselines.

Figure 6(b) examines how these gains behave as the amount of calibration data changes. RegMean and RegMean++ estimate Gram statistics; once these estimates stabilize, additional calibration samples make little further difference, and both curves plateau early. SLOA’s cross-state behavior-matching objective, by contrast, continues to benefit from additional samples, since more calibration data improves alignment across a broader range of inputs. The isolated sequential-correction baseline again outperforms RegMean and RegMean++ throughout, consistent with the component ablation above. Composing the QK and OV operators, however, is what allows their retained rank to be increased beyond what the original per-matrix factorization permits, and doing so yields a further, consistent gain over the isolated sequential baseline at every calibration budget. Sequential correction and operator composition are therefore complementary rather than redundant: the former limits the accumulation of merging error across depth, while the latter supplies the additional capacity needed to represent the union of task-specific directions once that error has been corrected.

Appendix G Computational Cost and Runtime Analysis

G.1 Merging cost versus baselines

Table 10 compares wall-clock merging time and accuracy across all methods when merging 20 task-specific ViT-B/16 checkpoints, using N=256N=256 calibration samples per task for the calibration-based methods. Being data-free is not synonymous with being computationally inexpensive: for example, TSV-M and Iso-CTS take comparable time due to concatenating weight matrices across different tasks and performing singular value decomposition. SLOA’s dominant offline costs are activation propagation through the merged network, solving the local operator objective at each layer, and defactorizing the composed operators back into weight updates. Critically, this cost is incurred once, when constructing the merged checkpoint: we pay it a single time, and the resulting accuracy gain persists over the model’s entire deployment lifetime. After merging, SLOA requires no task identity, routing, test-time calibration, or online adaptation – the merged checkpoint is used exactly like any single fine-tuned model. Increasing the retained rank rr increases merging time only modestly (from 175.95s to 186.74s, from r=64r=64 to r=256r=256), since it enlarges the local operators being solved and defactorized rather than introducing new computation; we quantify the resulting effects on memory usage and inference cost separately below.

G.2 Scaling cost with task count and calibration budget

Tables 11 and 12 characterize how merging cost scales along the two axes: the number of tasks being merged, and the calibration budget. As the number of tasks grows from 8 to 20, accuracy decreases on both backbones, reflecting the increasing interference among a larger and more heterogeneous task pool, while merge time grows roughly in line with the number of task-specific checkpoints that must be processed. Accuracy improves monotonically with more calibration data on both backbones. Peak GPU memory usage is reported in Tables 13 and 14. GPU usage is a function of the number of parameters, the amount of data processed for operator alignment, and the number of tasks we need to merge. ViT-B/32 stays under 6GB across every setting tested, while ViT-B/16 grows to 20.2GB at N=2048N=2048, still within a single modern GPU budget.

G.3 Inference cost

Table 15 isolates the cost of deploying the merged model itself, separate from the one-time merging cost reported above. Since every baseline in Table 10 merges by combining weights within the original 64/64 attention-head architecture, all of them, share an identical inference profile: throughput of approximately 3257 images/s, 0.307 ms/image latency, and 0.60GB peak memory. At the default rank (r=64r=64, no expansion), SLOA’s merged model is indistinguishable in inference cost from every baseline, while still improving accuracy to 82.37%. Rank expansion to r=128r=128 or r=256r=256 increases inference time and GPU memory, both direct consequences of the wider attention head, in exchange for further accuracy gains (83.53% and 83.74%, respectively). This is a deliberate, user-controlled trade-off between capacity and test-time cost.

Computational resources. We performed our SLOA merging method and conducted all the ablation studies, including benchmarking on a single NVIDIA DGX A100 with 48 GB memory.

Appendix H Task-wise full tables

This section reports the per-task results behind the averages in the main paper. Tables 17, 18, and 19 extend Table 2 with task-wise accuracies for ViT-B/32 merged over 8, 14, and 20 vision tasks, respectively. Table 16 likewise extends Table 3 with the per-task scores for RoBERTa on the seven GLUE tasks. All methods share the setup of the main experiments: calibration-based methods use N=256N{=}256 samples per task, and SLOA is reported at the original rank (r=64r{=}64) and with rank expansion (r=128r{=}128). SLOA’s average gains are broad rather than driven by a few tasks. Data-free methods use no calibration data, so for fixed checkpoints and hyperparameters, their merged model, and therefore their accuracy, is the same in every run; we report standard deviations only for calibration-based methods, where the variation comes from the random draw of calibration samples.
